Before the orders of the day are called I would like to ask the government whether their attention has been directed to a cable despatch setting forth a very important statement by the Prime Minister of Great Britain. It appears that In answer to a deputation which waited upon members of the British government to advocate the removal of the cattle embargo, the Prime Minister expressed himself in a very sympathetic way and stated that if he were convinced that live cattle could be admitted safely he would be in favour of abolishing the embargo. He also stated that if after consulting his colleagues he found any good purpose could be served by holding the inquiry requested he would grant it. Having regard to this very important statement respecting a matter that has often engaged the attention of the House and of the government I would like to know whether it is the intention to open up communications with the British government for the purpose of demonstrating-as I believe we can demonstrate-the absolute safety of the admission into Great Britain of live cattle from Canada. Is it the intention of the administration to open communications with the British government for the purpose of undertaking to demonstrate, as I believe they can, the absolute safety of admission into Great Britain of live cattle from Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not believe that anything could be done which has not been done long ago. When Sir Charles Tupper was High Commissioner for Canada, we demonstrated that there was absolutely no danger in admitting Canadian cattle and that our Canadian cattle were absolutely free from infectious disease. We do not admit that there is anything of that character existing in Canadian cattle and simply stand on the ground we have always maintained. So far as I know the difficulty does not lie in that direction ; but if the Prime Minister of England expressed himself in that way, we shall take note of what he said and if anything can be done, it will be.

If the report in the ' Free Press ' is accurate, his statement

seems to point to a new condition and call for further action.
Mr. AYLESWORTH moved the third reading of Bill (No. 115) to amend the Dominion Elections Act.

Before the third reading I wish to make a few remarks to remove the impression that seems to have gained currency in connection with the making of the new lists in the province of Ontario. We are told over and over again that these are to be judicial lists, made by judges. To my mind that is absolutely absurd. The judges are not going to make the lists in New Ontario any more than they make them in the older parts of the province. The judges are the final court of appeal and that is practically all that they will be in New Ontario with the exception of the fact that the enumerators, who are to form the lists in the first instance, are to be named by the judges. Beyond the fact that the enumerators are appointed by the judges instead of the Lieutenant Governor in Council, the judges themselves have nothing whatever to do with the making up of the lists. I was very much surprised to find the right hon. the First Minister take exception to the making up of these lists by enumerators appointed by the Lieutenant Governor and yet be willing that they should be made by enumerators appointed by judges. Both the Lieutenant Governor and the judges are the appointees of this government. Wherein then lies the difference which makes the one preferable to the other ? Should we not have just as much confidence in the Lieutenant Governor of Ontario, the chief magistrate of that province, the highest official in it ? Are you going to say that we have no confidence in that gentleman but we have confidence in the judges ? To my mind the judges occupy a secondary position compared with that of the Lieutenant Governor. My desire is to dissipate the idea that these are to be judicial lists. That is entirely erroneous. The judges practically will have no more to do with the making of the lists than I will, until the lists go to a court of appeal, and possibly only in a few districts will there be an appeal. So that all that the judges will have to do as regards the making of the lists in the new districts of Ontario will be comparatively trifling, and I do not want the idea to go abroad that these lists Will be purely and simply judicial lists made by the judiciary. Of course we are told that the judges are all angels without politics. If they are, I have not discovered any. I generally find that the judges have politics in Ontario as well as other people. I do not say that they exhibit any political feeling offensively,
but no man can get rid of the idea that he was once a Liberal or a Tory, and there can be no doubt that in appointing these enumerators the judges will have to appoint Grits or Tories. Whom they will appoint I do not know. Where they will get their recommendation I can conceive. I do not suppose that the judges know who are the best men to appoint as enumerators, and they must get their information from some source. What that source will be, I can only surmise. No doubt there will lie plenty willing to offer advice, perhaps unsolicited, and the judges will no doubt be aided materially. I do not say that they will be improperly influenced, but the enumerators must be Grits or Tories. They certainly will not be judges who will make up the lists in the first instance. All the judges will have to do will be to decide whether a man should be stricken off the list or added when there is an appeal. Let us get rid of the idea that these will be Heaven-born lists made by angels in the shape of judges and that nothing can be wrong about them. If that be the character of the lists, they will be extraordinary lists-a little more so than those in the older Ontario. I can see nothing in this Bill which will give the people greater confidence than they have in the Ontario law under which the Lieutenant Governor appoints the enumerator.

I do not think any good purpose can be served in my doing more than reiterate my protest against section 1 of this Bill. The attitude of the government is wholly inconsistent with its professions and absolutely irreconcilable with the circumstances in that northern country. I move in amendment:
That this Bill be not now read the third time but be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House for the purpose of amending the said Bill, especially section 1 thereof, so as to provide that the provincial voters' lists in the province of Ontario, whether in organized or unorganized districts, shall be regarded as of equal force and validity for the purpose of the federal election as those of other provinces, and so as to avoid any discrimination against the province of Ontario in that regard.

My only object in rising is to place on record what the position of the present administration was in 189S and show clearly where this government stood on the question now before the House and as embodied in the amendment. I desire to read two short extracts from the speech of the Prime Minister in 1898. The first is from ' Hansard,' page 4015 :
But I would not have hesitated to accept the franchise provided by a Conservative legislature in Quebec, because, though there were many things in that franchise, on the whole, to which I would have objected, still as it satisfied the province it would have satisfied me. It is in the same way as regards other

provinces. It is possible that the control of the several provinces may pass into the hands of the Conservative parity; still on a question of this kind I am quite disposed, for my part, to accept the franchise prepared by the legislature, whether Liberal or Conservative.
Then, the right hon. gentleman went a little further than that. Some hon. member, speaking on this question a few days ago- I am not sure that it was not the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson)-said that the position of his party at that time was based upon the fact that the lists were to be municipal lists. But here is what the Prime Minister said in 1898 as reported at page 4312 of ' Hansard ' :
We do not submit such a proposition ; we do not want the lists prepared by our appointees. We are satisfied to have them prepared by either the provincial or the municipal authorities.
Of course, it is in order for the present administration to be inconsistent-they can be inconsistent if they desire. I am not now referring to wliat took place before the Liberal party came into power, but what took place in 1898 when they decided to accppt the provincial lists as the basis of the franchise ; and in this second quotation which I have given, it is clear that the intention was to accept the lists of the provinces whether municipal lists or otherwise. I have risen only to make these quotations and to protest once more against the action of the government in discriminating against the province of Ontario. I repeat what I said : I believe that the province of Ontario is as competent to make voters' lists as any other province in the Dominion. If we are to accept provincial lists for Dominion elections, let us not discriminate against Ontario; if this government, or any other government, wishes to make Dominion lists let it apply the same rule to all the provinces of the Dominion.

It would be sufficient to observe to my hon. friend that in this legislation there is not intended to be, nor is there, any discrimination against the province of Ontario. The amendment put is rather insidious. Let it be remembered that the Bill refers only to the unorganized portion of the province of Ontario. I have stated before that there is good and valid reason why this was done. There is no proposal whatever in the Bill which is now before us for its third reading to attempt anything with regard to the Ontario lists prepared for the organized portions of the provinces. But the provisions of the Act now in force in Ontario for the revision of the lists in the unorganized districts lays this parliament altogether at the mercy of the provincial authorities. It is provided, under the law passed in 1907 and now in force, that the Lieutenant Governor in Council may pass orders whenever it suits their Mr. KEMP.
purpose to prevent registration taking place in the unorganized portions of the province. They can prevent the revision of the lists this year, or next year, or the following years. In fact, at the present time, there is a proclamation by the provincial government to prevent the revision of the lists in the unorganized portions of the province. Then, what will take place ? That will take place which has taken place in the past- that is, there will be no revision of the lists for two or three years. In the province of Oninrio, in 1904, no provincial lists were provided except those of four years before. We had to make our own lists, and we had to do it in a hurry, giving no satisfaction to the people at large, as has been shown by the facts brought out in the debate on this Bill. Therefore, it is far preferable that we should have power to make our own lists as the Bill provides. And this is represented as an attempt against the province of Ontario. I was more than surprised when I heard my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol) telling me here across the floor that I should be the last man to invade the privileges and rights of Ontario. I cannot see why I should be selected in this way or what was the irsinuation or innuendo of the hon. gentleman in making such a charge against me. There is no such intention. The attempt is made here to create the impression that we are invading the rights of the province of Ontario. My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) went so far as to say that the changes would be rung on this theme in every town, in every village, in every township in Ontario. I know the province of Ontario, I think, as well as if I had been born in that province. In this matter I know I can rely on the good sense of the province of Ontario against this cry. The people of that province know that when their rights are invaded they can defend those rights ; they are not to be gulled in this way when there is no attempt against them.

I think the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid 'Laurier) will find that the people of Ontario are not to be * gulled,' to use his own words, by any such statement as that which he has made. It is idle for the Prime Minister to say that there is no discrimination against Ontario, because this Bill which it is proposed to put on the statute-book shows precisely the reverse. On -what is this discrimination against the province of Ontario based ? Is it based upon the idle statements, unsupported by any evidence, recently made in this House and relating to only two of the six ridings of northern Ontario ? Is it based on that, or is it based on something else ? These hon. gentlemen do not seem to know. I now put the question squarely to them across the floor, and not one of them knows how to answer. And no wonder, for, as a matter of fact, this

legislation is being placed upon tbe statute-book, upon the demand, the imperative demand, of two of their partisans in this House, and for no other reason. The Prime Minister declares there is no discrimination! Are there not lists made in other provinces in Canada by enumerators and revised by judges ? And are not these left as good and valid lists for federal purposes without any interference by this parliament ? On what ground is this legislation affecting the unorganized districts of Ontario based ? Is it based upon the fact that the lists in those portions of Ontario are not municipal lists ? There are lists that are not municipal in British Columbia, in Manitoba, in some parts of Quebec, if I am not mistaken, and in Prince Edward Island. None of these are interfered with. But in the unorganized parts of northern Ontario, where lists of precisely the same character are made up and revised by judges, these are selected by (the government for the purpose of special treatment and discrimination. There is no doubt about it. The pages of the statute-book, when this Act goes into effect, will demonstrate what I say.
The Prime Minister resorted to another argument which is quite as fallacious as tbe one to which I have just alluded. He says that the Ontario government can prevent the lists from being made up, and therefore it is necessary for this parliament to interfere by legislation. He is apparently, when he makes that argument, either ignorant or forgetful of the provision of his own statute, because section 7 of the Dominion Elections Act as it at present exists, makes provision for that very contingency. It is not necessary to read it again, it has been read over and over again. I challenge contradiction by the Prime Minister, or any other gentleman on that side of the House. Section 7 of the Dominion Elections Act makes provision already for that very contingency which the Prime Minister puts forward as the reason for this enactment. Hon. gentlemen opposite will not challenge that assertion because they cannot. Anv challenge of that kind would be followed by the reading of the section which makes that special provision. Therefore, so far as that argument is concerned, it falls to the ground.
There is therefore no other alternative for the people of this country to accept than the one which is set forth in this resolution, namely, that by tbe legislation now before parliament, and which this government by its majority intends to drive through, special discriminatory provision is made in respect of six northern ridings, and that is done without a shadow of pretense o- excuse except the hearsay statement put forward in this House by two hon. gentlemen sitting on the government side. It .'s not necessary to repeat this, it has been made abundantly plain to the people of this 420
country. I venture to think that if no better excuse for that can be put forward than that which has been urged by the Prime Minister, the people of Ontario will not be likely to regard this provision in that kindly light which has been predicted by my right hon. friend.

The right hon. gentleman says that there is no discrimination in this legislation against the province of Ontario. I venture to think that not only is there discrimination against the province of Ontario in this legislation, because legislation already exists which provides for making the lists by the federal government if the lists are moie than a year old in Ontario and throughout Canada, but discrimination is obvious from the fact that all these alleged reasons which are advanced by every one else than the Prime Minister, came into existence after this legislation had been planned and brought down to the House. That seems to be overlooked by the Prime Minister. In that legislation at first, Ontario and Quebec were coupled so far as the unorganized districts were concerned. 'But now Quebec is left out and Ontario is left in. I want to say to the Prime Minister that he has discriminated against the province of Ontario in another way, a way which is contrary to the courtesy which he has always shown to gentlemen on either side of politics, or anywhere else, and that is in the fact that he was not above communicating with the premier of Manitoba and the Manitoba government in reference to the lists of Manitoba, when a strong protest was put up in this House. But did he communicate with the premier of Ontario, or the Attorney General of Ontario in reference to this legislation or these complaints 1 Not a solitarv communication of any kind. I have been informed by the Department of the Attorney General of Ontario that there were not three persons affected by all .these alleged complaints that have been made in this House. So I wish to reiterate that I think it would have been in accord with decency and harmony if the Prime Minister or the Minister of Justice, instead of allowing his supporters on almost the last day of parliament to make these unsupported statements before this House, had courteously communicated this complaint to the Attorney General of Ontario and asked to have new lists framed, as there is power to frame them, if there was anything in these complaints, on or before the 1st of July. But no complaints have been made to the Attorney General of Ontario and the usual proclamation lias been issued stating that it is unnecessary to go to the expense of having another revision two months later in these northern districts, and now special legislation against the province of Ontario is being enacted. It would have been a simple matter to place



these alleged facts before the Department of Justice of that province and have an investigation, and if there was found to be anything wrong, I am sat'sfied that there is not a man in this country who does not believe that the Ontario government would have done justice to the hon. member for Rainy River or any other member.

In addition to that, the Prime Minister of Ontario and the Attorney General of Ontario offered to have new lists made up under the pi-ovincial laws in any ridings where any serious irregularities were shown. They were prepared to do that, and that was well known.

So, >Sir, I think the animus of the right hon. gentleman and his government is shown by one passage in his speech where he said that he did not propose to leave this House to the mercy of the provincial government of Ontario. ' I was astonished that he should use language of that character in reference to a matter of this kind, if he was desirous of showing that he was not discriminating against Ontario. I leave it to this House and to the people to say whether the right hon gentleman is not discriminating against Ontario, both as regards this legislation, and as regards the ordinary business treatment and courtesy that one government should show to another.

I have stated on a former occasion, and I repeat it now, that there is no attack whatever upon the government or the province of Ontario with reference to provincial lists. I cannot for the life of me find by what process of reasoning hon. gentlemen opposite can persuade themselves that there is anything in this Bill that reflects upon the province or the government of Ontario. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Bristol) stated further that the reason that the proclamation was issued, if I understood him correctly, cutting out the preparation of the new lists, was because no complaint was made against the lists. The hon. gentleman is aware that during the recent provincial election the Liberal press in the ridings were full of complaints, and these complaints led to official proceedings. I read to the House a few days ago the evidence given at a trial that took place in the district of Thunder Bay. and I sent that report to the leader of the opposition. I was surprised to hear that hon. gentleman say to-day that no evidence had been given to this House, nothing but mere assertion, but no positive evidence of a sufficient character that there was anything wrong with the lists.
BORDEN The statement which the hon. member submitted to me was merely a report from his own solicitor.
That is correct. My honoured friend believes a lot of things on

testimony. I suppose he believes that there is such a place as the city of Jerusalem. But did he ever see it ? What evidence has he that there is such a city ? He believes it on testimony. I submit there is ample testimony as to the wrong preparation of these lists, showing that they were of a partisan character. That fraud was committed upon the opposite political party is amply established by testimony. We have not had a committee. We have not had men here to examine them. If my hon. friend wrishes to take advantage of a legal technicality of that kind, well that is a lawver's privilege. It is only a quibble though. 'The fact that there has been testimony cannot be denied, my hon. friend can treat it in any way he pleases, but I make the statement knowing that it is correct that the result of this investigation is that Mr. Cummings' lists have got to go through the procedure that the law requires. Under the ruling made by the judge, before whom the case was heard, Mr. Cummings has been informed that he must post up his entire list, not _ subdivisions of it, that he must give notice in the public press as the statute provides, that the fifteen days must now run and that he must make the affidavit that he has done this before the judge can give a certificate.
If it is the case that the matter is being dealt with by the judge under the provincial laws, and if the laws are thus being remedied, why should this parliament interfere?

I am very glad that my hon. friend asked me that question, because that is the serious part of the whole situation. I made a statement with regard to Mr. Cummings' list. I am told that the same condition exists with regard to Mr. Hogarth's list. Mr. Hogarth never published any notice, never posted up a completed list, never gave the people notice that it was posted up and never made the affidavit that the law requires him to make in order to obtain the certificate that the statute calls for. My hon. friend says that this shows that you have a legal procedure by which he can deal with these lists. That is only so as to two divisions. What about the twenty or thirty other divisions in which legal proceedings have not been taken in time to bring out these facts? The door is closed.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman why the same proceedings were not taken to invoke the powers of the judge under the law, and if it is to be expected that this parliament will interfere whenever people do not see fit to avail themselves of the remedies which are at their disposal?

Why should it be necessary? Why should the voter be put to the

expense of forcing law suits, and expensive litigation, against tlie province to get his rights ? That would be a sufficient answer, but the answer has already been given. The law was changed, the people did not understand the 'amendment by which the time was cut down to fifteen days. This amendment was passed at the last moment, in the closing hours of the legislature ; it was not an amendment to the Voters' List (Act or to the Election Act, but it was an amendment to the Statutory Land Amendment Act. I couud not get it. I could not find a lawyer in Port Arthur or Fort William who had it, who knew anything about it, or who could give me any advice with regard to it. Under these circumstances, I am surprised indeed that the hon. leader of the opposition or hon. gentlemen opposite do not consider that such legislation as that now before the House is necessary. Is it that they desire to obtain a partisan advantage? What are the conditions which call for this legislation? As to the reason for the legislation, my hon. friend said that the Dominion statute provides machinery for preparing lists even if the province of Ontario did not prepare lists. That is not an answer to the argument that this legislation is necessary, because it is admitted that the machinery has proved defective. Hon. gentlemen opposite complain against it. The hon. gentleman behind him (Mr. Boyce), on several occasions, has declaimed loudly against it. I would like to know now if my hon. friend is prepared to say that he will be satisfied with the existing law.
It is perfectly obvious that the proper thing to do in that ease is not to make a discrimination against the province of Ontario, but to amend section 7 in the way my hon. friend suggests.

My hon. friend will see that the province of Ontario is the only province in which the lists were ever prepared under the Dominion law, and under those circumstances where is there a discrimination against Ontario? When the lists were prepared in 1894 nobody ever thought of such actions being a discrimination against Ontario because they were prepared there and nowhere else. The reason is that the conditions existing in Ontario do not exist elsewhere. In the province of Quebec it is not the legislature that prepares the lists, but the counties. In Prince Edward Island, I am told, they have no lists at all, that a man simply gets a ballot and votes. In the Northwest there are different conditions. Ontario presents the only conditions with which we are compelled to deal, and now that we are dealing with them I cannot see that there is any justification for the assertion that we are discriminating against or offending Ontario. Why should the Ontario government be offended?
420}
Because you introduced the Bill before these reasons existed.

Not at all. That is only in the mind of the hon. gentleman. It has been introduced upon sound principles. But hon. gentlemen say that the Ontario government will be offended. I would like to know upon what ground? Has the Ontario government gone into politics to assist gentlemen opposite by preparing stuffed, fraudulent or illegal lists for the purpose of dictating to this House who its members shall be? I do not believe it. I do not think that the Ontario government would hold for a moment that it is their business to interfere with the rights of this parliament. Provincial rights exist, but the question of provincial rights in this House only arises where the undoubted privileges and rights of the legislature are invaded. I would like to know how it is invaded by this Bill. It is within the competency of this parliament to pass this Bill, and there is no question of provincial rights involved in it.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this matter has been so largely discussed on the motion for the second reading and in committee that I have very little to say, but I wish to make a few remarks by way of answer to some of the objections that have been urged to this proposed change in the law. I think that an important consideration is to remember what the existing law is, to compare the proposed change with the existing law and to judge by that comparison whether or not there is an improvement in what is now proposed, and whether or not, therefore, what is now proposed ought to be accepted. Under the existing law the lists for the unorganized portion of the province of Ontario will be prepared anew in accordance with the provisions of the existing statute if a Dominion election at any time fail to be held at a period of more than twelve months after the preparation, in this portion of Ontario, of the provincial lists. That law as applied to this unorganized portion of Ontario has been , subjected, in this House, in the e course of the present debate and previously, to very severe criticism as being a provision of the statute which, if not altogether unworkable, it is at all events, impossible to work out satisfactorily. Of necessity, that provision of the law must be worked out after the writ for any Dominion election issues, because, up to the very date of the issue of the writ, no man can tell whether or not there will be a provincial list not too old to be used at that election.
If the provincial list at the date of the issue of the writ is less than 12 months old. it is to be adopted under our present statute and it is only when such provincial list is more than 12 months old, at the

Hate of the issue of the writ that a new list is to be prepared for that portion of the province under the provisions of the Dominion law. Accordingly it is only after the issue of the writ that those steps can be taken under the present provision of the law. That time, it is said, will not be adequate and in any event the men by whom that new list is to be prepared will necessarily be selected by the Dominion government. Those objections have been urged more than once to the present law as applicable to the new or unorganized portions of Ontario, if there should be a necessity for relying upon that law.
In the condition of things which we have to-day as to the unorganized portion of Ontario, it is at least of equal probability that in case the present Bill is not passed the provisions of the existing Dominion law would have to be invoked to obtain a voters' list at the next Dominion elections. The provisions of the present provincial law as to the unorganized territory require the work of the enumerator to be done during June, he has to begin on or after the first day of June in each year unless his work is dispensed with, and he has to conclude on or before the 30th day of June. During June in the present year that work was not done ; it had been done before June or may have been in course of completion during the first week of June just passed. On the 30th of June a proclamation was issued dispensing with the preparation of any lists for the unorganized territory during 1908, no such preparation can now take place under the provisions of the Ontario statute, so that if a Dominion election comes to be held at any time during the present year or at any time in the year 1909 before or during the month of June it would be impossible to have any list for that Dominion election unless you took the list prepared under the existing provincial law to which such serious objection has been raised. If the Dominion elections are held before June next it would be possible of course to adopt, if any one were so minded, the lists which have been prepared during the spring months of the present year by the provincial authorities and which have been discussed here. I do not intend to go into any discussion of these lists beyond pointing out that when objection was made to their character the answer that came was simply ridicule of the statements of members on this side of the House as to the character of those lists and the manner in which they were prepared. The statement was made by the hon, member who has just spoken that these lists have been prepared and published in sections, the enumerators certifying them in parts or in sections, from time to time as new sections or parts were prepared. The statute plainly contemplated only one list, only one certificate when it was completed, and one period Mr. AYLESWORTH.
of 15 days after the whole list was completed within which appeals from that whole list might be taken. It was said when objections were made that they were entirely without foundation, they were absurd, and this list was a right* good list. The hon. member who was making these statements has now demonstrated at the end of judicial proceedings that this list is utterly incorrect, utterly illegal and stands exactly as it left the enumerator, not having been subjected to any judicial revision whatever, and being but an improper, incomplete and entirely imperfect list upon which to run an election. The moment that is demonstrated as the result of a judicial inquiry the whole ground is shifted and you hear the cry : Why do you not go on with your appeals ? In the meantime an election has been carried on on a list of that character, and if the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Oonmee) had not gone to the expense of a judicial inquiry by which he has established their utter illegality and impropriety these very lists, in the absence of legislation now in question before this House, would have been forced upon him or any other Dominion candidate for that constituency. That is the kind of inspired, heaven-born list which hon. gentlemen opposite say is immensely superior to a judicially prepared list, for the preparation of which all necessary time will be given and all proper means and facilities afforded for correcting it before the judges of the country.
The issue here is simply whether the existing law is to continue or whether this measure is to be substituted for it. A great deal has been said about an insult to Ontario by the proposition made here. I reply that I have exactly as good a-right as any other member in this House to speak for the province of Ontario. I do not recognize any better right on the part of any hon. gentleman opposite, no matter who he is, to speak for Ontario than I claim for myself. I think further that I am speaking here not merely for myself but for at least 38 other members of this House from Ontario who are here supporting this measure, and if we are insulting anybody it certainly is not the province, or the whole province of Ontario by any means. We constitute more than 45 per cent of the representation of the province of Ontario in this House and speaking for more than 45 per cent of the electors of Ontario I resent the arrogance of hon. gentlemen opposite who talk about an insult to Ontario.
It is said that we ought to have communicated with the provincial government of Ontario before we introduced this Bill. I would like to know what more the provincial government or legislature of Ontario has to do with the means by which we shall regulate the preparation of voters' lists for elections to this House than we in this House have to do with the means whereby the provincial government or legis-

lature of Ontario shall regulate its own franchise. We have just as much right in this House to control our own franchise and our electoral lists as the legislature of Ontario has to control its lists and its franchise, and there was no more reason why we as members of this House should consult the legislature of Ontario before proposing any legislation we saw fit with regard to the preparation of our lists than there was why the government of Ontario should have consulted us before passing their Voters' Lists Act last session. There was no more want of courtesy in the one case than in the other ; the one legislature is as indenendent as the other in the preparation of its lists or in regulating the means whereby the franchise will be determined for elections to its own house. Hon. gentlemen have attempted to work up great indignation and to represent this as a matter in which some insult has been offered to Ontario or some discrimination made against it. If hon. gentlemen opposite think they will receive any benefit at the polls from this stage performance they are perfectly welcome to it. It is a measure which I should be happy to discuss before any assembly of electors, and I am perfectly willing to meet any hon. gentleman on the subject at any time or place and discuss it before any audience in Ontario.
When this measure was first introduced we heard a great deal from hon. gentlemen opposite about its operation as applied to the little province of Manitoba and the plea was made :	You are afraid to take
somebody of your own size. We do not hear that now, there is no whine or cry of imposing on the little province of Ontario but the ground is shifted and now it is said: Here is some intolerable insult that is being flung into the fact of a majestic, a mighty and a great portion of this Dominion. It seems to me the two lines of argument are hardly consistent, and when added to all that the effort is made to show that by reason of some sinister influence within the cabinet or out of it. there has been some effort to discriminate against Ontario in favour of some other portion of the Dominion, surely the ridiculous has come to its fitting conclusion.
Why in Quebec there are no lists whatever in respect to the unorganized territory. Indeed, according to the argument of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) there is no such thing as unorganized territory within the province. At all events no lists have been prepared within that territory and to-day if there are residents there entitled to vote they are not upon any list. It is not then a matter of choosing between provincial lists and Dominion lists so far as that province is concerned, it is a matter simply of considering whether or not this parliament should step in and as to that part of the province of Quebec do what its own local legislature has, up to this time, not seen any necessity for doing. If there is any call or necessity for the preparation of lists in that portion of Quebec which is known as unorganized, and if the provincial legislature applies to that portion of the province a method of preparing the lists different from that which obtains in the remainder of the province, as unworkable or as unlikely to work satisfactorily, as unlikely to produce a fair and impartial list as experience has demonstrated the provisions of the similar law with regard to the province of Ontario are, then it will be time for this House to consider whether or not the lists so prepared for the unorganized portion of Quebec are lists which this House ought to accept as determining its franchise for the purposes of elections to this House. But that time has not yet come and until there are lists prepared in some shape or other and until it is a question whether or not those lists so prepared shall be accepted for that portion of the province of Quebec, there was no occasion for this provision so far as that province was concerned.
When this Bill was originally introduced, it applied to all portions of this Dominion, not already provided for, in regard to which the lists were not prepared in accordance with the system pointed out in our existing election law. That was objected to, the measure was, so far as Manitoba was concerned, modified, as gentlemen know and I need not go over those circumstances again. That modification taking place, the complaint now is that we have retained not the original measure but a measure modified as proposed by the leader of the government six weeks ago, referring this question to judicial determination, and because we have retained that so far as Ontario is concerned, this prolonged objection to the present proposed provision is now made.	_
The hon. member for Halton' (Mr. Henderson) this morning says that this is no real judicial preparation of the voters' lists. I can only refer him to the language of the Bill which, if passed, it will fall to those judges themselves to interpret, and which is certainly worded as plainly as any words I am able to find could make it. This Bill provides that the board of registration shall appoint as many enumerators as are necessary and that the duty of those enumerators shall be to do their work how? Under the supervision and in accordance with the directions of such board of registration. I do not think those words are by any means meaningless. They were inserted for a purpose and I believe that before any body of judicial interpreters they will have full effect. I do not mean to say that the judges themselves or any of them will go from house to house like census enumerators looking personally for the voters or registering them, but I do say

that having appointed some men as their substitutes, or delegates, as their appointees to do that work, the preparation of t|he lists will be done by those men under the actual supervision of and in accordance with the actual directions which may be given from day to day or for that matter from hour to hour, if that is necessary, by the judges themselves. And these judges are therefore under this statute as literally to prepare these lists by themselves as Is the man who builds a house literally doing that building if he stands there day by day and sees the workmen laying the bricks, building the stairways and putting on the roof. It is true they do not do the work with tjheir own hands, but it is being done under their immediate direction and supervision by men appointed by themselves and under their entire control. I maintain that it is in every respect a judicially prepared list as effectively as though the actual work of enumeration was done by a judge's own hand.
5 The bon. member for Halton has gently, but still unmistakably, conveyed to the House and to all who may read his remarks the impression that although a judge has accepted and is in discharge of his high judicial duties, he cannot, be does not, forget the political alliances which may have existed in his case before his appointment to the bench. So be it. If my hon. friend in seriousness means it, if he thinks it, so be it. We have in this territory of New Ontario six constituencies and nine district judges. Three of their number were appointed before the present government came into power. I say nothing more than that with regard to political affiliations, but I do remind my hon. friend from Halton that if out of nine judges in Ontario there are three appointed under such circumstances as I have pointed out, there is, proportionately at least, exactly the same representation that hon. gentlemen have to-day in the political complexion of this House. I say then that we are here talking of this work of the judges of the land as we find them. I know that no more impartial tribunal could possibly be selected for the work that is in hand, and it reduces itself simply to this point, that the objections which have been taken to this proposition in committee and here to-day mean that hon. gentlemen opposite believe all voters' lists perfect so long as they are prepared by political partisans selected by hon. gentlemen themselves or their political associates while if such lists are prepared by political partisans selected from this side of the House, then such lists are utterly objectionable. But even if such lists are prepared by impartial judicial authorities, they are equally to be condemned because nothing will satisfy hon. gentlemen opposite unless they can prepare with their own hands the election lists upon which we appeal to the electorate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: I wish to say a few words in reply to the observations of the Minister of Justice. The hou. gentleman claims that he has as good a right to speak for Ontario as any member in this House. Well, in this connection, I do not think he has as good a right to speak for the province of Ontaiio as the men who were here years ago when the Liberal party put itself on record, time and time again, by declaring that the provincial lists, and no other, were the proper lists to be used. That was the stand taken by the present First Minister, by his colleagues who were then in the House, including the late Hon. David Mills and the Hon. Edward Blake. Men of the greatest prominence and importance in the Liberal party of that day declared over and over again that the provincial lists, and no other, were the lists to be used in the Dominion as well as the provincial election. That was one of the planks of their platform on which they went to the country. But in this Election Bill, the government are deliberately setting aside that principle as regards the province of Ontario. They deliberately refuse its application to the unorganized districts of that province. That would not be so bad if the province of Ontario was the only one which had unorganized districts. But other provinces also have them. The same condition exists in other provinces in that respect as exists in Ontario to-day, yet there is no application of this Bill to them. Is it not an insult to Ontario that she should be thus discriminated against? I say it is a deliberate insult to the province of Ontario that this Dominion government refuses to trust to the honesty and integrity of the Ontario officials or the Ontario administration. In the face of this measure, the Minister of Justice cannot claim to speak for the province of Ontario. What is the reason for this? The right hon. the First Minister says the object is to give a man in the unorganized territory a vote by providing for the making up of a list in that territory where now there is none. But if that be the case in the unorganized districts of Ontario, it is equally the case in the unorganized districts of the province of Quebec. Yet he has made no such provision for that province. There he is willing to leave the matter in the hands of the local government, but Ontario, for which province he claims to speak, he treats differently.
Are you the protector of these men in the province of Quebec?
Where does the hon. gentleman say that occurred?
In the Algoma district I heard the botfst made by D. A. Macdonald himself.
Under what government?

The Mowat government. I am speaking of what is a matter of historical fact to-day. I heard the man who did that boast of it on the Pacific boat coming down the lake in 1892. That was one of these devices on which the hon. member for Rainy River has always depended for election. In fact the Bill now before the
House ought to be called the ' Conmee Bill,' because its main object is to secure the election of that hon. gentleman. It is because of the knowledge of these things that we are to-day resenting the insult offered to the province of Ontario. We all remember the tricks that were resorted to by that hon. gentleman in the past and I am sure his right hand has not since lost its cunning. At one time it was the ' Minnie M,' at another D. A. Macdonald, and at another something equally disreputable.
To-day these bon. gentlemen opposite desire to be in a position to do what their friends boasted they would along the line of the Transcontinental The minister, however, has yielded to the strong arguments against the Bill, but nevertheless now, at the tail end of the discussion, he talks very violently against those who compelled him to amend it. Why did not he address these arguments and reproaches to the House weeks ago ? He dare not, because he knew they would be answered. But to-day, because he knows that time will not permit an answer, he becomes very valient and very important. But the people of Ontario will remember, when the day of retribution comes, and, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth), the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and their friends will be punished by the electorate, when that electorate has an opportunity to pronounce its verdict upon this Bill which is being forced upon the House.
I would like to ask the hon. member a question.

I do not intend to delay the House for more than a moment, I wish to call attention in the first place'to a paragraph which I find in the editorial column of the Toronto ' Globe ' of Saturday, July 4, to which my attention has been directed only recently. The paragraph to which I allude is this :
There need not much he said regarding the Dominion Elections Bill, which has at last reached the committee stage in parliament. But, in the interests of truth, it should he put on record that the concessions which the opposition now declare to be satisfactory were offered early in May last. The time since wasted might far 'better have (been devoted to serious public.business.
I am inclined to agree with the principle enunciated in the last sentence of this extract, but in so far as the statement of alleged fact in the second sentence is concerned, namely, that the concessions alluded to were offered to the opposition early in May, I desire to say in all sincerity, that the statement has no foundation in fact whatever and that it is absolutely devoid of truth. I do not say this by way of Imputing any desire of misleading to this journal but simply to place the matter on its proper basis as far as tbe facts are concerned.
I have already, in Committee of the Whole House, moved a resolution foivthe amendment of the Bill now under discussion by way of providing that the poll in a general election in Canada shall be held in every constituency on the same day except in so far as the Yukon Territory is concerned. By section 80 of the Dominion Elections Act five electoral districts are excluded from the general rule. As to certain of these there may be some question, but as to others I think there is no question. The Kootenay division of British Columbia, at least, according to the statement of Mr. Smith Curtis, the Liberal candidate for the riding should not be included iu this list As far as other British Columbia ridings are concerned, I have the same information. My information with regard to them has been controverted by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. As far as the Kootenay riding is concerned, I am supported not only by the provincial government of British Columbia, not only by the circumstance that the provincial elections are all held on the same day In that province but also by the statement of Mr. Smith Curtis, to whom I have referred. I will not take up further time in discussing the subject, but I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Bristol :
That the Bill he not now read a third time, hut be referred 'back to Committee of the Whole House with instructions to aimend the same by making provision that at every general election in Canada the day for holding the polls shall be the same day throughout Canada except in the Yukon Territory.

It may properly be inquired, why, having regard to what I have said just now with respect to the difference of opinion between the two sides of the House, I make the motion in this way. My answer is that my hon. friend from Prince Edward county (Mr. Alcorn), in the amendments which he introduced into this House in this Bill and which were proposed as amendments to the Bill now before the House, pointed out a simple and easy way by which these five constituencies could be brought within the general rule. The difficulty arises, I understand, in all eases with respect to the posting of the proclamation and by adopting the means pointed out by my hon. friend for Prince Edward there should not be the slightest difficulty whatever in fixing one day for the whole of Canada.

I agree with the hon. member from Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn) that his estimate that the proclamation should be twenty-three days In the hands of the returning officer before nomination day is a reasonable one. If he gets it twenty-three days before nomination day there will be sufficient time except in Comox-Atlin if the returning officer happens to live in Atlin. But, does not my hon. friend see that if it requires twenty-three day's before the nomination it must necessarily require twenty-three days after tbe nomination so as to distribute tbe ballot boxes and swear in the returning officers? That would make forty-six days from the time that the returning officer receives the proclamation until tlie poll can be held.

I am obliged to confess, and I trust my hon. friend (Mr. D. Ross) will not blame me for doing so, that I do not see anything of the kind. As a matter of practice in every constituency it is known and will be known perfectly well that the election will not be by acclamation and that a poll will be demanded. It will neither be necessary nor desirable for tbe returning officer to sit down and wait for nomination day for he knows perfectly well that two candidates will be nominated and he can make arrangements accordingly As a matter of fact in my own province of Nova Scotia, long before nomination day the returning officer makes his arrangements with his deputies. In the county of Halifax, which is 140 miles long and where men have to come a distance of 120 miles in some cases, this is always done and it can be done in these ridings in British Columbia just as well. I do not think there would be the slightest difficulty In adopting'the proposal of my hon. friend from Prince Edward.

The hon. gentleman must see that in a district such as Yale-Cariboo the ballots must be printed at some central point after the nominations are held, and his suggestion that the returning officer might anticipate what was going to happen on [DOT]nomination day does not apply to British

Columbia. We do not know until nomination day whether a socialist candidate will be nominated. They might make up their mind the day before nomination to place a candidate in the field. Then, the ballots must be printed at, say, Kamloops, the ballot boxes must be distributed from that central point and consequently the work cannot be done in a shorter time than the proclamation can be posted from any settled point.

As far as that is concerned my hon. friend from Prince Edward was not fixing twenty-three as the minimum time, but he was fixing a period of twenty-three days as a time which would be absolutely ample in all constituencies.
No, I do not think so.

Well, it is not worth while to bandy contradictions across the floor of the House. I have said all that I have to say on that point. I think there is some difficulty to be encountered, but in so far as the Kootenay district of British Columbia is concerned, there is absolutely no difficulty at all if we are entitled to rely upon the statement of Mr. Smith Curtis who says that there is not only no necessity, but that he does not desire any postponement in that riding.

We have been accused of doing this to get a political advantage, but so far as I am personally concerned I do not think there is much dishonour in getting beaten in an honourable way, and I would much rather have the election on the general election day and take chances. I believe if the election is held on the same day as tl.e other elections you will have your organization better in hand. But, the district of Yale-Cariboo is 700 miles in length from the United States boundary to the Alaskan boundary and it contains 175,000 square miles, while the district of Kootenay contains about 29,000 square miles. So far as Kootenay is concerned, if Mr. Curtis Smith wants his election or the same day, I think it can be arranged, but in Yale-Cariboo and Comox-Atlin-X know the districts well-it is a different matter. It is absolutely impossible to hold the election in Yale-Cariboo on the same day unless the proclamations are issued at least 60 days before the day of polling. If His Excellency can dissolve the House and wait 60 days fur an election then I am perfectly satisfied? Notwithstanding the telegram read by the leader of the opposition from Premier McBride, the fact Is that the provincial government found it absolutely necessary to pass an older in council deferring the election in the provincial district of Skeena for two weeks after the general election because it was impossible to get the ballot boxes into that district. I know the leader of the opposition wants to be fair and I tell him it is absolutely impossible to hold an election in Yale-Cariboo unless 60 days elapse between the issue of the proclamation and the polling. There are nine provincial electoral districts in Yale-Cariboo and the provincial elections are . arranged from nine different centres, while in the Dominion election they must be arranged from one centre for that large area. Under the provincial election law the deputy returning officer makes a declaration before any two voters who happen to be there, whereas under the Dominion election law the deputy returning officer must be sworn in before a justice of the peace and :n many instances there is not a justice of the peace within 100 miles of where the poll is held. It is more difficult now than in 1904 to arrange for an election in that constituency because people have gone into Stewart lake and Chapel valley along the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific in northern British Columbia where there are no transportation facilities. It will therefore take you a much longer time than in 1904 to provide that the settlers in that remote area shall have their votes recorded.

I assume that the hon. member (Mr. Duncan Ross) knows of the amendment placed upon the Votes and Proceedings of the 29th of June containing the scheme set forth in Bill (No. 80) with regard to this subject. He is perhaps aware that part of that scheme is that in these five at present excepted constituencies the nomination day is advanced one week, and (hat therefore 14 days will elapse between the nomination and the polling.
That is not enough.

If it were true, which I believe, it is not, that the ballot boxes must necessarily be distributed from one common centre for the whole electoral district, there are 14 days in which to perform that service and surely that would be sufficient. But, I believe that nowhere in the Dominion are there Dominion ballot boxes specially provided. The practice is to use the ballot boxes used in the provincial and municipal elections and therefore there is no distribution to be made except within a very restricted area. The only thing the returning officer would have to do would be to distribute his ballots, and I believe 14 days would be sufficient for that, even in as large a constituency as my hon. friend has.

But, under the Act, ibe ballot box which is received by the returning officer must be sealed, must contain a copy of the election law, must contain sufficient ballots for the polling subdivision, and must be opened by the deputy returning officer in the presence of two electors. If that be so the argument of my hon. friend (Mr. Alcorn) falls to the ground.

My hon friend is entirely mistaken. The ballot box is only sealed

by the deputy when he returns it to the returning officer.

The Magdalen islands are attached for federal purposes to the county ol' Gaspe and at certain seasons of the year it is next to impossible to communicate with them. The electoral district of Chicoutimi extends to the Labrador coast and in certain seasons of the year the obstacles to communication in that district are almost insurmountable. I call the attention of the leader of the opposition to the fact that it is certainly impossible to have the elections in these two districts held at the same time as in the other constituencies.

When special conditions arise at certain seasons of the year the elections can be held at a later date under section 91 of the Dominion Elections Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have discussed this matter as fully as I' wished on the second reading of the Bill but I might point out that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) seems not to have his own political party behind him in the position which he now takes. I suppose no more pronounced exponent of Conservative political views in this country can readily be found than the Ottawa * Morning Citizen,' and I read from the Ottawa ' Morning Citizen ' of the 27th of June last the following brief editorial :
In some of ithe recounts of the votes passed at the recent provincial election, ballots have been thrown out because of mistakes on the part of returning officers. In other cases officials who Should have been 'better instructed have jeopardized votes by irregular markings of the voting papers. That is, to say the least, unfair. The ballot represents the will of the people and that will should rule. No 'mistake of an intermediary should thwart the expression of the peoples' opinion. The sins of the returning officers or those responsible should not be visited upon the voters.
I concur in every word of those sentiments and It was in that view that I framed the amendment which is in question.

The Minister of Justice has set us an edifying example by reading newspaper articles when we are endeavouring to hurry through the business of the session. I do not know how much progress we shall make if other ministers follow that example. He appears to be of the Mr. ALCORN.
opinion that in voting for this amendment we desire to vote against any fair proposal to ensure that no man's franchise shall be taken away. We do not propose anything of the kind, but we do think that section 17 as it stands, for reasons which have been abundantly pointed out in this House is likely to lead and I have no doubt will lead to results which are not desirable. I do not minimize the difficulties which have been brought to the attention of the country in the Wentworth and three or four other cases but when you can point to only five cases since 1867, a period of forty-one years, surely the grievance is not so great as to justify a remedy to which some exception at least can be taken. However, the matter has been threshed out to a wearisome extent in the House.

I do not know where the leader of the opposition gets the idea that there have been only five cases of the kind since confederation. I know of three cases in my own county and in the last provincial election in Quebec there were over five cases, most of them proved in court.
Your deputy returning officers must be very stupid.
In two of the cases they were Tories, I think in all three.

I still think that this clause should be struck out of the Bill. It may be that errors will occur and that deputy returning officers may make mistakes, and in that way some candidate may be deprived of a seat to which he is properly entitled, but I consider that a very small matter indeed compared with the hundreds of thousands of electors throughout the country who are forced by means of a clause like this into voting against their consciences and therefore I cheerfully support the amendment and hope the House will throw out the clause.

Under the present law cannot the same thing occur as will occur under this? Cannot the deputy returning officer make marks? Then how many instances have been brought to light in which the manner of voting has been discovered by such a mark.

I know of my own knowledge that where the law permitted the manner in which a voter voted to be known as has been the case in Ontario for the last thirty years, voters' lists were taken to Toronto, were marked from the original ballots and were used again in a subsequent election which occurred in the same year and that marked list was used for the purpose of coercing votes. I know as a matter of fact that voters were coerced. One man applied to me on election day and asked if I believed they could discover how he voted. I was obliged to tell him they could, that the law permitted it and I had

no doubt In the world they did know how he voted in the previous election and would in that election. He said this was unfair, as it would compel him to vote as he did not want to. That was no doubt done repeatedly throughout Ontario with working men. I will not support any law that would take away the independence of the electorate and lead to the coercion of voters.

This same question has been taken up in the United States and it has been held there in reported cases that a state law which would render a vote invalid by reason of any mark or error of a deputy returning officer would be unconstitutional.

I was uot in the House when clause 22 was debated, or I would have had the benefit of the opinion of the legal gentlemen iu the House on it. I would direct attention to line 15 of section 22. From my standpoint this clause adds to all the iniquities of the old one by making out a candidate to be a criminal merely because some agent of his, without his knowledge or concurrence, did something which the candidate would have prevented him from doing had he any knowledge of it. Everybody will concede that the Act, as it is, was sufficiently stringent, and that it contained a number of severe restraints and grievous punishments which perhaps were out of all proportion to the wrong done. I notice that line fifteen provides that the actual personal expense of any candidate, his expenses for actual professional services performed, shall he held to be expenses lawfully incurred. Is there any limitation in the amendment to the Bills which can be rendered by professional gentlemen for services in an election ? Is there any limitation to these services they can perform 1 Perhaps the legal gentlemen handled this question very gingerly. It seems to me that this is handing over the whole representation in the House to the legal fraternity.
No layman would pretend to run an election when he can be made liable to imprisonment and fine because of the actions of an individual of which he has no cognizance. This is intended to put the whole control of the electorate in the hands of solicitors. A solicitor, who acts as agent for a candidate, can do all the things we are trying to. prevent by this Bill. These angels who, we are told, are held in chains under darkness, awaiting the great day of judgment, must, I think, be given an intermission in their nains to laugh over this Bill. We are enabling a candidate to get around the penal provisions of this Act by allowing his solicitor to do everything forbidden in it. In England a candidate does not pretentd to do any of these things. His agents do certain things but his solicitor does the rest and presents a Bill for so much for his work. In England the bill is rendered by the solicitor for professional services. The price is ten pounds for every voter who votes and five pounds for every one who refrains. The angels in the bottomless pit must laugh to find us making Acts, creating offences and at the same time asserting provisions which enable them to be avoided-setting up pains and penalties for certain acts and then devising machinery by which the whole measure can be nullified.
