GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolutions :
1.	Resolved, That the government of Canada may aid and assist tho construction of a line of railway of the Edmonton, Yukon and Pacific Railway Company, hereinafter called the company,' from a point on the company's line of railway, or on the line of railway of the Edmonton and Slave Lake Railway Comp'any, at or near Edmonton or Strathcona, in the province of Alberta, thence in a generally western direction, to the coal areas, situated at or near the Brazeau river and the headwaters of the McLeod river, for a distance not exceeding one hundred and fifty miles, by guaranteeing the principal and interest of the bonds, debentures, debenture stock or other securities, hereinafter called ' securities/ secured as hereinafter mentioned, of the said company, or of its successors by amalgamation

as hereinafter provided, to the extent of thirteen thousand dollars per mile for the first fifty miles of the line so aided, and for the remainder of the said line, to the amount of twenty-five thousand dollars per mile, not exceeding in all one hundred and fifty miles, the interest upon the said securities to be at the rate of three and one-half per cent per annum, payable half yearly, the principal to be payable in fifty years.
2.	Resolved, That the said securities sd guaranteed shall be secured by a deed or deeds of trust, by way of mortgage or charge, to a trustee or trustees, approved or by the Governor in Council, and such deed or deeds of trust shall respectively grant a first mortgage or charge upon the said line of railway so aided, and the right of way, station grounds, or other real estate and interest therein, buildings and other structures and improvements, rolling stock and equipment, plant, machinery, tools, supplies, materials and other personal properties, present and future, acquired for the purposes of the said line so aided, and in connection with operating, repairing and maintaining it, and the tolls, incomes and revenues of the company arising and to arise from the said line, and the rights, privileges, franchises and powers of the company now or hereafter held with respect to and in connection with the said line and the operation, maintenance and repair thereof.
3.	Resolved, That the deed or deeds of trust shall create a mortgage, or charge, upon all other lines of railway and properties of the company, and upon all the property and franchises, tolls, incomes and revenues connected therewith, to rank thereon next after the bonds, debentures, debenture stocks or other securities theretofore issued by the company, and next after any existing deed or deeds of trust by way of mortgage or charge securing them ; Provided always that with respect to lines of railway or parts thereof now constructed and in operation, for the mileage of which no bonds, debentures, debenture stock or other securities have yet been issued, the company may issue first mortgage securities at a rate not exceeding twenty thousand dollars per mile, and may secure them by deed: or deeds of trust by way of first mortgage or charge, having priority over the mortgage or charge created by the deed or deeds of trust hereinbefore mentioned.
4.	Resolved, That the kind of securities to be guaranteed as aforesaid and the forms thereof, and the form and terms of the deed or deeds of trust securing them, and the times and manner of the issue of securities and the disposition of the moneys to be raised thereon, by sale, pledge or otherwise, pending the expenditure of such moneys for the purposes of the line of railway so aided, and the forms and manner of guarantee, shall be such as the Governor in Council approves of, and such terms, provisions and conditions may be included in such deed or deeds of trust as the Governor in Council deems expedient or necessary.
5.	Resolved, That the said guarantee shall be signed by the Minister of Finance or such officer as is designated by the Governor in Council to sign it; and upon being so signed the government shall become liable as guarantor for the payment of the principal and interest of the securities so guaranteed according to the tenor thereof, and the said payments

shall form a charge upon the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
6.	Resolved, That the rates and tolls charged by the company upon any of its lines shall not in any case be higher than the rates or tolls fixed in the contract to be made between the government of Canada and the company.
7.	Resolved, That any moneys paid by the government of Canada under any guarantee herein provided for, shall be held to be paid in discharge of the liability of the government and not in discharge of the liability of the company under the securities so guaranteed, or under any deed of trust securing them, and the moneys so paid shall be held to be still secured by the said securities and deed of trust, and the government shall be subrogated in and to all the rights of the holders of such securities, the interest upon or the principal of which has been paid by the government, and the government shall, with respect to all moneys so paid, be in all respects in the position of security holders with respect to whose securities default has been made in payment to the extent of the moneys paid by the government.
8.	Resolved, That the guarantee of securities as herein provided, for the said line of railway shall not be given until the Edmonton, Yukon and Paeifio Railway Company and the Canadian Northern Railway Company have amalgamated into one company under Ithe name of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, nor until the amalgamated company, as successors by such amalgamation, has become, as maker of the securities, liable for the payment of the principal and interest of the securities so to be guaranteed with respect to such line of railway.
9.	Resolved, That the decision of the Governor in Council as to the length of the mileage of the said line of railway so to be aided, shall, for the purposes hereof, be final.
10.	Resolved. That the books of the company shall at all times be open for inspection for and on behalf of the government by any person named in that behalf by the Governor in Council or the Minister of Finance.-Mr. Graham.

I think the minister should outline the policy on wh'Ch he grants these bonuses. He should explain why he grants bonuses to some railways and none to others, why he chooses to guarantee the bonds of certain railways instead of giving bonuses. Personally I am opposed, and have been for years, to these bonuses. It is too late in the session to discuss the matter at any length, but 1 would point out that when hon. gentlemen opposite wei*e in opposition they found great fault, and justly so, with this way of proceeding. These bonuses resolutions should be brought down at such a period that we could have an opportunity to fairly investigate them and make our arguments for and against them as the case may be. I wish to put on record my protest against this way of doing business and against all bonuses to railways.

These resolutions do not refer to bonuses. I am not referring at all to what has been the policy of the govern-

ment, but this position I do take. In a new country like Canada, development depends largely on transportation and transportation depends largely on railway construction. In order to develop a new country and enable those who come to it, as well as those who reside in it, to get the best return for their labours, railway facilities are necessary. We have not arrived at the point when we can have all the facilities we desire without government aid. When discussing any railway project, we have to decide whether it is better to give it so much per mile or guarantee its bonds. In the case of a company with considerable resources, my own opinion, especially in the case of trunk lines, is that it is better for the country to guarantee the bonds, because then we are not taking any risks. But in the case of the smaller lines perhaps the better way is to give them some cash aid, and they only get that after the line is constructed, on the report of the engineer. So that, if we get no railway, we pay no money. The only matter to be discussed, to my mind, in connection with this would be whether Canada has arrived at the point when we can do away with aid to railways. My own opinion is that Canada has not arrived at that point. I have endeavoured to deal with every application on the merit of that application, so far as I could get the information necessary.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I desire to say one or two words on this subject, and, perhaps, for the sake of the economizing time, I may make a few observations also with regard to the resolutions which follow. These resolutions were presented to the House seven months and seventeen days after this session was opened. The House now, within forty-eight hours of prorogation so far as we are able to learn, is invited to consider these resolutions and pass them. There has been a great deal of complaint, especially from the Liberal press of the country, and some from hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, as to the length of this session, and we have been told that the work in which we have been engaged should not have occupied a longer time than five months. Either this government has been holding back for more than two months and a half resolutions which it deemed perfectly proper, or else it is bringing down now certain resolutions which it does not really believe to be in the public interest. There is the alternative. Do hon. gentlemen opposite seriously contend, in the face of this proposal, brought down more than seven months and a half after the opening of the session, and only after repeated requests by the opposition for their early presentation, that they have to blame hon. gentlemen on this side for the delay ; or are they not forced to admit that the delay during this session
has been due to the inability of the government to deal with public business in a businesslike way and to bring their measures before the House in proper time? What is the answer ? Were these subsidies decided upon three or four months ago? Was the government ready then to bring down these subsidies so that we might complete our work within five months after the session had begun ? That is the question they will have to answer for themselves and as to which, I venture to think, they will not be able to answer satisfactorily.
What are the proposals that the government brings down? The first is a proposal to undertake bond obligations to the amount of $11,067,000. The government brings that proposal down to the House on the afternoon of Thursday, and it intends that this House shall be prorogued on Saturday afternoon or evening. That is, forty-eight hours before the time fixed for the conclusion of this session, the government bring down a proposal that the country should incur bond obligations to the extent of eleven millions and upwards. But that is not all. They bring down railway subsidies embracing revotes of subsidies for nearly 1,700 miles of road and new subsidies for nearly 2,300 miles of road-subsidies for a total of nearly 4,000 miles of railways. The combined length of all the lines of railway proposed to be subsidized under these resolutions would extend from the Atlantic to the Pacific across Canada. Therefore, this is a proposal to subsidize railways equal to a transcontinental railway. And the government asks parliament to take up that subject seriously after seven months and a half of the session has passed, and within forty-eight hours of prorogation. It is perfectly obvious that the government are not disposed to have serious discussion or consideration of this proposal-they know it is impossible. If their proposal was ready at the time when this session, according to their own views, should have come to an end, then for what reason is it that they did not present these measures to the House months aeo? Look at the amount of aid involved; 3,935 miles of railway at $3,200 a mile amounts to about $13,000,000, which it is proposed to take from the public treasury and use in subsidizing various lines of railway throughout the country. But the proposal is not limited to $3,200 per mile. For if any of these railways is built at the cost exceeding $15,000 a mile, a greater subsidy is given. Looking over the aid granted to railways throughout the country during the last three years under resolutions similar to these, I find that the average amount of aid is over $5,000 a mile. If you take $20,000 a mile as the average cost of these roads-I do not think that would be an unfair or exaggerated assumption-you will find that instead of $12,592,-

000, the public treasury is pledged by these resolutions to no less than $22,566,300. This with the amount of bond obligations proposed by the resolutions now under discussion make a total of $33,500,000 and upwards, which parliament is invited to seriously consider within forty-eight hours of prorogation. And this we are invited to do without any correspondence having been brought down, without any documents being laid on the table which are of much value. It is true, the Minister of Railways has laid upon the table, or rather, has furnished to myself, and, I believe, to some other members, a memo, with regard to the bond guarantee which we are now invited to vote. But still I venture to say the House is absolutely without any information whatever which would enable it to fairly consider and determine whether these individual subsidies ought to be voted or not. I rise for the purpose of making an earnest protest. I do not think that the action of the government in leaving the introduction of these resolutions to the last moment is fair to parliament or to the country. Furthermore, I would say it is not fair even to themselves. Surely conditions are not such that these subsidies, or at least ninety-nine hundredths of them, were not resolved upon two or three months ago. If so many of them were resolved upon at that time, why were they not brought down in time for reasonable discussion? But the government have left all of these resolutions to be brought down at this time. And I protest that it is absolutely impossible for parliament, at this stage of the session, to give to these proposals the consideration which in all justice to the country and in view of the magnitude of the proposals, should be bestowed upon every one of them.

When I saw these resolutions on the Order Paper, although I knew we had very little time before us, I determined that I would not let them pass without criticism. I want particularly to speak in reference to the new subsidies. The other portion of the resolutions is objectionable, but not so objectionable as the new subsidies. In reference to guarantees, I can understand that there may be conditions under which it would be right to guarantee certain sums for railway enterprises. But there is no time now to consider whether such a course is or is not correct in reference to a particular matter. The amount we have already guaranteed for railways is very large. The amount we are now asked to guarantee for these railways, as has been said, is some $11,000,000. By these resolutions we are also taking over the Quebec bridge, the loss in connection with the Quebec bridge and undertaking to provide the money required for the building of a new one. We are by this resolution also revoting a large amount upon enterprises to which we were Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
committed before. 'At a moderate estimate, these revotes will amount to about $10,000,000. The history of railway building in 'Canada I do not think justifies us in assuming that any of these railways to which we are committing ourselves will cost less than $20,000 a mile on the average. There is no justification in subsidizing a railway unless it is one of peculiar difficulty in regard to construction, and I think we can assume from the fact that the Transcontinental Railway costs us more than $00,000 a mile that these railways we are now subsidizing will cost on the average at least to the limit of our liability or $21,400 a mile. On that basis, the revotes will amount to more than $10,880,000. But * I wish particularly to speak of the new subsidies. According to my calculation the lines total 2,267 miles, according to another calculation they amount to 2,235 miles.

I think I did state 2,235 miles. But the Minister of Finance told me that about 35 additional miles were to be included, and my estimate was made up on the first basis and without taking into consideration the 32 miles which have since been added.

That would make my calculation correct. In paying $3,200 per mile up to $15,000, it amounts to $7,254,400.
I assume that it will cost probably double that amount, it may cost $45,000. We pay $3,200 per mile on an expenditure of $15,000 per mile, and on any expenditure over $15,000 we pay half the cost, not exceeding in all $6,400 per mile.
How does the hon. gentleman make up those figures, when the maximum amount is $6,400 per mile? It does not matter what it costs afterwards.

For a cost of $15,000 per mile we pay $3,200, above $15,000 we pay one half of what it costs, not exceeding $6,400 per mile. Now, if we pay $4,800 per mile we shall pay on these new subsidies $10,881,600, or if the limit is reached, nearly $15,000.

I do not understand the hon. gentleman's method of computing those figures. The subsidies are paid upon the cost of the railway up to $21,400 per mile. If a railway costs $60,000, or $70,000, or $80,000, it makes no difference to the country.

If the hon. gentleman does not understand my figures I understand them, and I think the country will understand them. Up to $15,000 we will pay $3,200 ; above that we will pay half the construction until the cost reaches $6,400. I am assuming, from the history of railway construction in this country, that it will cost at least $18,200 per mile,

and if it does we will pay $4,800 per mile, and the total cost will be $10,881,600. I say that the conduct of the government cannot be justified in bringing down at this stage of the session a proposition committing the country to such an enormous expenditure. Aside from the subsidies we are revoting, we have about 2,270 miles of railway in regard to which we are committing ourselves to a probable expenditure of $6,400 per mile. I submit that it is absolutely unjustifiable. I submit that the time has now come when we should not be paying subsidies for the construction of railways. Having regard to what Canada has already done in railway construction, I say we are not justified in paying one dollar of subsidy to any railway. The proper position for the government to take is this, that the circumstances of this country are such as to lead to the unaided construction of railways wherever they are a national or a commercial necessity. Many years ago in the United States they adopted that principle, and I have no doubt that the good sense of the people of Canada will say that the time is entirely passed when we should be subsidizing railways.

As a representative of a rural constituency, I desire to enter my protest against the huge amount now being voted for railway subsidies. I believe that the constituency I represent is opposed to these subsidies; and personally I am opposed to them. I believe the time has long gone by when we should advance such enormous sums to subsidize railway companies. If we compute the sums of money that have been granted, both by this parliament and by the legislatures of the various provinces, by way of bonuses and subsidies to railways, they will amount to enough to build those roads almost entirely, and the result is that, although the people of the country have paid for the roads, the railway companies own them. I am opposed to these bonuses. I think It was not wise on the part of the government to bring down an important question like this within forty-eight hours of prorogation, when there is no opportunity to discuss it clearly and intelligently. We are reaching a point in our expenditure when we should call a halt, and when we consider that we are to-day asked to vote about $30,000,000, I think it is more than the people of this country expect us, as their representatives, to support. I wish to express myself as strongly as I possibly can in opposition to these subsidies. I think it is an imposition upon the people, and they will not show themselves to be in favour of it when they are asked to record their votes in the coming election. There must be some reason why this huge sum is asked. It is very apparent why we are asked to vote this money. I think we all know that 421
there is an election coming on, and that that accounts for this large amount of money that is being voted. As the representative of a rural constituency, I wish to oppose this expenditure. When we consider that we are voting, in general estimates, bounties to lead, railway subsidies and other grants, no less a sum than $227,000,000, hon. gentlemen will agree with me that it was time to stop and consider the situation. We are running expenditure mad ; it Is time to call a halt, and I want to express my opinion in opposition to this extravagant and unwise expenditure for railway bonuses. The Minister of Railways and Canals tells us that in a new country like this it is necessary to grant railway subsidies, but why is It necessary in the old sections of the country, especially In Ontario, which are well served with railways, to continue granting subsidies? If the railway companies feel like building roads in competition with lines already built, they should pay for these roads themselves and not ask the government of Canada to subsidize them.
I would like to ask the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) to be good enough to tell us how many lines of railway he has in his county?
I think we have the Grand Trunk and Michigan Central.
You are-doing well.
Certainly, we are doing well.
In some counties we have none at all and we would like to have some.
Is that any reason why we should grant subsidies where there is plenty of competition?
Will my hon. friend tell me if the railways in his county have been subsidized?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Before these resolutions are disposed of, I wish to put myself on record as being unalterably opposed to them. As far as I can judge the sentiment of the people of Canada to-day they are opposed to subsidizing railways. Expressions of opinion have been given by various bodies from time to time in the last few years and especially by the agricultural class indicating that they are opposed to subsidizing railways. It cannot be other than well known to the government that this is the feeling of the farmers to-day. They believe, as I believe, that we have reached a time in the history of the country when, if more railways are needed, we should depend on private enterprise to supply the capital to build these railways and leave those who invest their money in them to depend on the earnings for their returns. We have ample evi-



dence that the railways will be built whether we subsidize them or not, because, in several instances, we have refused to allow capitalists to come in and build roads in Canada and supply the necessary capital themselves. In view of that fact and in view of what I believe the sentiment of the people of Canada to be I am opposed to these resolutions. I am opposed to them as well because of the stage of the session at which they are brought down are submitted to this House. If there is any merit in one or more of them the date is too late and the data which should be available for our purpose is not available to enable us to analyse these propositions and to determine which are meritorious and which are not. They should be weeded out and analysed, but it is entirely too late to do this. It is committing the country to enormous undertakings without a proper analysis or the proper information that we should have before we give our assent to these resolutions. I am opposed to them as well because I fear that they are proposed to-day for one purpose more than any other and that is for the purpose of using them as bribing agencies in view of the approaching elections, enabling hon. gentlemen opposite to dangle them before the people of the country in various districts and to say: You should return the government to power again because of the assistance which they are giving to a railway through your county. Even in gratitude you ought to support the government, but if you do not support the government you are not likely to get as much assistance in the matter of construction of railways as you will if you do support the government candidate. Having regard to our knowledge of how elections have been run in the past by the present government we are justified in coming to the conclusion that these resolutions will be used to their utmost to assist the government in carrying very many constituencies.
I think the government has another object in view as well. This means has been adopted by the government at the present time for the purpose of raising a large campaign fund from these subsidized corporations to enable them to run their elections. Some may not take that seriously and some may, but I say that we have had in the history of Canada cogent examples that justify us in reaching that conclusion today. We believe that we are on the eve of an election, that the government are preparing to bring on the election in the very near future, and the history of the past affords us ample justification for reaching the conclusion that this is one of the means whereby governments raise large sums of money to corrupt the electors and carry their candidates to power when the election comes on. Therefore, I say that, if for no other reason, it is not an opportune time to allow these resolutions to pass. I think the country's attention Should be drawn to these ' Mr. SPROULB.
facts. Why are the government guaranteeing the Canadian Northern Railway as they are doing to-day? Is there any justification for it? Have we any evidence that the people are in favour of their doing it? We have lately passed through a provincial election and the condemnation which was, over and over again, heaped upon the Whitney government by friends of the federal government in opposition to the means adopted for assisting the Canadian Northern Railway, and the fact that on platform after platform they denounced it in the strongest language, this proves one of two things-either that the Reform party were absolute hypocrites when they said that they didl not believe it was justifiable to assist the Canadian Northern or they are hypocrites to-day, because they will go before the people of Canada and justify it to a larger extent than was proposed then. They will do to-day what they condemned a few weeks ago.	Will they
support it to-day? Of course they will, and they will go out and support it in the country notwithstanding the fact that many of them went on the platform and condemned it with regard to the assistance that was proposed to be given to the Canadian Northern Railway by the Whitney government. They are adopting the same means to-day, but they are adopting it to ten times greater extent than was proposed then. It was wrong then it cannot be right to-day. Hon. gentlemen who condemned it then cannot consistently support it now. I am opposed to it andl I believe the people are opposed to it. They have put themselves on record time and time again that they are opposed to the further subsidizing of railways. There may be some justification for continuing grants that may have been given to enterprises that are now under way. But that is no justification for providing large subsidies for a number of ne^v enterprises as set forth in these resolutions. I desire to put myself on record in opposition to this, believing, as I do, that the people of Canada are opposed to further subsidizing railways at the present time.

The criticism which I shall now offer will apply to the resolu-lions generally, as I do not propose speaking at any other stage. The Minister of Railways has told us that the time for aiding railway enterprises has not yet passed, and, that is one of the most justifiable things the hon. gentleman has said in this House. But I disagree with him entirely as [DOT] to the manner of aiding railway enterprises. It has been the practice in by-gone years for a few men to organize a railway company , and then appeal to the federal government, i to the local governments, and to the muni. cipalities for aid so as to secure money . enough to construct the road. As a general

thing those engaged in railway promotion never expect to invest a dollar of their own money. I believe the time is past for municipal bonuses and I also believe the time has passed for federal and provincial bonuses. We want railways in Canada, and if we are going to get them they must be aided, but that aid should be given in the form of a government guarantee. X approve of that principle, and I do not see why the government should not apply it to all these different railroads as well as to the Canadian Northern. In the recent Ontario elections the Whitney government was criticised for guaranteeing the Canadian Northern bonds. I justified that guarantee and I am prepared to justify it to-day, because I believe that the true principle of aiding railway enterprise is for the government to guarantee the bonds. Why should the people of to-day put their hands in their pockets to build a railway that is going to serve the people of fifty years hence ? I think we should leave some responsibility for those who come after us. If we guarantee the bonds and the bonds are unfortunately not redeemed by the company, then our descendants who benefit by these railways will contribute towards the expenditure, and the whole burden will not be thrown upon the shoulders of the already over-burdened people of today. We were told by the Liberals when in opposition that ithe people of Canada were being bled white at a time when the annual expenditure of the country was only $40,000,000, but what are the people of Canada going to say to these enormous expenditures being heaped one on another at a time when our annual outlay is $150,000,000. I protest against these bonuses ; I do not intend to support any of them. I think it is time the government should call a halt.

I feel it my duty, notwithstanding the desire to get through the business of the House, to enter my solemn protest against this bonusing of railways which is condemned by the farmers throughout the length and breadth of Canada. One of the strongest planks in the Liberal platform of former days was that railway bonuses should cease, but the Liberals in power have forgotten that. The ' Farmers Sun,' the most able organ of the farmers of this Dominion, has condemned railway bonusing in the strongest possible manner, and in that opinion of the ' Farmer's Sun ' I cordially concur. And not only that, but it is worse still that in the dying hours of the session with prorogation in sight the government should bring down this enormous expenditure. If the government had submitted their measures months ago instead of waiting until a short time before prorogation the business of the House could have been disposed of long ago. The Ross government for years pursued a policy of delay in a similar way, but the Conservative opposition forced them to bring down their measures in proper time 4211
to allow of proper consideration. Here we are rushing millions and millions of the people's money through without due consideration. I believe, Sir, that the people of Canada will at the first opportunity retire from power the government which imposes such enormous burdens upon the people and which shows such procrastination in submitting measures to parliament.

The Minister of Railways has been most unfair to this parliament in delaying until the last moment the submission of these resolutions. It is now impossible to ascertain the facts and consider the proposals, as they should be considered. It appears ito be the policy of the government to grant bonuses to and to guarantee the bonds of railway companies, and that being their policy the Minister of Railways should have pressed for a grant of aid to the Ottawa and Brockville Railway which is a most important and necess-sary line. The capital of this Dominion has practically no direct railway communication except that which is afforded by the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I believe it would be a great help to the people of the district through which this railway runs as well as to the city of Ottawa if the Grand Trunk Railway Company had direct communication with the capital. The Minister of Railways has neglected the Brockville and Ottawa line, and as to that I would not complain at all were it not that he has subsidized railways in other parts of the province of Ontario which are not go much in need of railway facilities. With that feeling and knowing that it would be of such assistance to the country and to Ottawa as the capital, I think the Minister has not been fair to us in this district in not seeing that aid was given to the railway proposed by this company. If that had been done I am satisfied they would have proceeded with the building of the road at once.

We have recently come through a provincial campaign in Ontario. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) spoke on the platform with the leader of the opposition in the legislature, Mr. A. G. McKay, and the whole complaint was that last awful week in Toronto. What was that last awful week ? The Hon. J. P. Whitney enunciated in his platform of 1904 the principle that not one dollar of bonus should be given to any railway in the province of Ontario. He adhered to that policy rigidly ; the only complaint wras that he undertook to guarantee certain bonds of the James Bay Railway to the extent of some $2,000,000. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) now asks this House not in the last week of the session, but in the last 48 hours to pass bonuses for millions of dollars and a guarantee of bonds for millions more. Personally I am not opposed to the guarantee of

bonds under proper conditions and proper circumstances. I believe it is the best way of assisting railways in opening and developing new territories and that history will show this country will not be called upon to pay one dollar of principal or of interest where the bonds are for a reasonable amount, and precaution is taken to see that the railway is built through a country that will likely be a good producing country. What I do complain of is the absolute hypocrisy of the party which went through Ontario condemning the Conservative party because the Conservative party guaranteed bonds to a small amount, and then asks us to-day, with 48 hours ahead of us, to grant bonuses to an extent of about $20,000,000. I have not had time nor has any hon. member to thoroughly investigate the bonuses to the different railways but I have run through some of them. In Ontario the Ross administration in its dying days granted a subsidy of $2,000 a mile to one railway which is now getting a subsidy of $6,200 a mile. The Ross government granted a land subsidy of millions of acres to another railway which is now getting a subsidy from these hon. gentlemen of $6,400 a mile. Under certain conditions it might be reasonable to grant certain bonuses. The province of Ontario in the past has done it, the Ross government left for the Conservative government a debt of five or six millions incurred in subsidies to railways. But since the advent of the Hon. J. P. Whitney to power in 1905 not one dollar has been granted in subsidies to any railway and yet the Liberals in Ontario raised the cry of that last awful week, simply because there was a guarantee of bonds which I believe was justified. I do not think it is possible for us in 48 hours to thoroughly consider these resolutions. We know we have to prorogue on Saturday and X with others feel that these resolutions should have been brought down weeks ago instead of being left to the last days of the session.

When, only a little over a month ago, hon. gentlemen opposite and their political friends throughout^ Ontario were making the welkin ring with their denunciations of that last awful week, to a certain extent I agreed with them. On the public platform in Ontario I said that while personally I agreed with the settlement of the mining suit and the guarantee of bonds under the circumstances and conditions under which the Whitney government had guaranteed them, I joined with hon. gentlemen of the opposite shade of politics in denouncing the Whitney government for passing such legislation in the dying days of the session. I feel that I am consistent to-day in protesting not merely as a Canadian ratepayer but as a member of this House, against the studied in-Mr. PRINGLE.
suit that is paid to members of this House by bringing down such important legislation in the dying days of the session. Not only is it impossible for us to give the proper consideration to these matters, but a blow is struck at the dignity of parliament itself. I venture to say there is not an hon. gentleman opposite any more than on this side who does not know that in the eyes of the great public of Canada the dignity of parliament is lowered and our influence is decreased by the fact that fourteen or fifteen hon. gentlemen who happen to occupy seats on the treasury benches can bring down such an immense grant at a time -when it is impossible for private members to vote intelligently, knowing that there is a sufficient number in the House who will be ready to vote blindly for whatever they may bring down. I appeal to supporters of the government to consider their own dignity, the respect we owe to ourselves as well as to our constituents and to protest against such enormous grants beioig brought down when the country knows we cannot understand what we are voting for. If they protest the Prime Minister must heed them.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to place myself on record as opposed to this resolution and I believe that in doing so I am voicing the strong feeling of the constituency which X represent.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with other members in condemnation of the government for their extravagance in voting such amounts of money for aid to railways in Canada. I notice the resol- . utions cover some ten pages of the Votes and Proceedings of to-day and if we do not protest against the action of the government we will have some member of it, possibly the Minister of Customs, in a few days saying that the opposition members allowed millions to pass without protest. That is the kind of government we have to deal with so it is necessary, even if we take a little time, to enter our protest against these extraordinary expenditures.
In my own county, during the last year and a half, we have had an example of a large railway corporation constructing an important railway without the aid of a dollar from the public treasury, Dominion or local; that is the new Canadian Pacific Railway branch from Toronto to Sudbury, which is looked upon as one of the best roads in Ontario. The roadbed is perfect and it is a credit to the company. If the Canadian Pacific Railway are able to construct a line from Toronto to Sudbury without public aid, surely the other railways of Canada can construct some of these branches without money from the public treasury. Therefore without having had an opportunity to look into

these resolutions and refresh my mind as to the geography in order to ascertain where the lines are to be constructed, and not knowing the local considerations, I wish in a word or two to express my disapproval of the large vote the government is asking this afternoon.
Mr. ALEXANDER MARTIN (Queens, P.E.I.) I raise my voice, Mr. Speaker, against these railway resolutions, especially against the bonuses. Considering the heavy obligations to which the right hon. the First Minister has committed this country-the Transcontinental which is to cost between $200,000,000 and $250,000,000 ; the Georgian Bay canal, $100,000,000 ; the Hudson Bay Railway, $30,000,000 to $50,000,000 ; the Welland canal, something like $30,000,000-considering all these I think it is high time he should cry halt. The late Sir John Macdonald gave this country the Canadian Pacific Railway, and his memory is green and will remain green in the minds of the people for what he has done. What he did then was very costly, but the Canadian Pacific Railway has come to be one of the greatest and most successful undertakings that Canada ever ventured into. But the First Minister is coming now to the last straw which is going to break the camel's back. With the credit of this country in the markets of the old world diminished, he goes on favouring certain parts of Canada for political purposes. It is all very well to say we are building up a great country, but are we not travelling too fast? Here are estimates amounting to something like $180,000,000, yet ten years ago, when our estimates only amounted to $42,000,000, the right hon. gentleman considered them entirely too much. In 1890 he condemned railway subsidies in toto. The time had come, he said, when they should cease. Is he going to do for Canada what the late Mr. Mercier did for Quebec ? I am afraid he is. When we consider the niggardliness with which he treats some provinces-my own for instance-and the lavish expenditure he proposes to make in others, I am at a loss to understand how the hon. gentleman expects this country to bear the burden. He is incurring expenditures which are staggering the country, which he cannot justify, and now he comes down at this hour of the session and asks us to swallow a host of railway subsidies without giving them at all any consideration.

Could I be permitted to add a word to the testimony of hon. gentlemen opposite, though not in the same direction ? I do not think that to-day in Canada the people as a rule are playing the part of Rip Van Winkle. They have had their eyes open for some time, and they realize that the conditions to-day are vastly -different from what they were some years ago. There is one thing of which they are certain, and that is that the status
of Canada at present is far better than it ever was during any previous year in our history. There have been two or three objections raised to these resolutions. The main one is with respect to the lateness of their introduction. Well, I have to commend the government for what it is doing. In this the government are in harmony with the ideas of the people. They are in harmony with the popular sentiment when they realize existing conditions and our future possibility. They have at last, in the interval between all these cries of scandal and motions and resolutions, which we have had from week to week, designed some say for the purpose of obstructing the business of parliament, been able to bring down, in the form of a resolution, certain propositions, which, to my mind, crystallize the best hopes and aspirations of our people. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) took one other exception, and it was that this was only one other means of bribing the people of Canada
Hear, hear.

But he said the right hon. leader of this House would realize that the people of Canada were opposed to anything of the kind. Sir, if that be true, how is it possible that these railway resolutions ean be offered as acts of bribery ? I think that my right hon. friend is too astute a statesman to propose to the people something which will not be acceptable to them. Reading these resolutions in detail, I find that the views of the west are being recognized, I realize that the views and hopes and aims of the people of central Canada are being realized. I further realize that those propositions, whether they relate to the east or the west or the centre, are acceptable to the people of Canada. Why ? Because Canadian citizenship to-day realizes that we are on the threshold of great possibilities.
They realize that responsibilities rest upon them, and they want a government in power that can understand the conditions and provide for them. I have been for many years allied with the Liberal party. I was an opponent of the party of the hon. gentleman opposite when it was led by that great statesman, Sir John A. Macdonald. I want to say this in tribute to his memory- though he needs no such tribute-that he grasped the situation and provided for its possibilities and requirements. And I congratulate the right hon. leader of this government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that now, when conditions are changed, when we have made rapid strides, when we have attained a higher plane and. enjoy a wider view of the possibilities of our country, he makes provision for these great interests. For that, I believe he will receive, as he merits, the approval of the citizenship of Canada. I do not wish to join hon. gentlemen opposite in holding a post mortem on the past.

But I would call the attention of the leader of the government to the fact that in the past we have aided railways, particularly In the eastern section of Canada and have spent large sums on the government system of railways. My hon. friend from Queens, P.E.I., (Mr. A. Martin), a few moments ago, condemned the incurring of liabilities in the settlement of the transportation problem. And yet, in the next breath, he complained of the disregard of the requirements of his own province in the same direction. The hon. gentleman, I am sure, realizes that Prince Edward Island has received attention, and so have the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec in connection with the government system of railways. As subsidiary to the government system, this parliament has, from time to time, given aid toward the construction of railways which should be branches and feeders of that government system, and these contributions toward railway construction have benefited materially the government system. These expenditures in aid of branches of the government system were made for the purpose not only of increasing the traffic of the Intercolonial but of aiding the communities which these branch railways serve. Now, Sir, the government, having met the requirements of central Canada, as it is doing by these resolution*, should turn its eye to the conditions prevailing in eastern Canada. I shall not repeat the arguments I addressed to the House on a recent occasion, but I ask consideration of this: Is it not in the interests of the Intercolonial from a business standpoint, that the government should acquire the lines connecting with the government system, to make those lines do more perfectly their work as feeders and so increase and extend the traffic of the government system and to benefit further the communities served by these branches? Now that we have under consideration these propositions in the interests of the transportation problem of Canada, I would ask if the government has considered the desirability of acquiring these lines as feeders, thereby perfecting the government system and fulfilling the hopes of the communities served by these branch lines ? I do not wish the government to confine itself to one province, but to consider every province. In Nova Scotia, there are branch lines which are recognized as peculiarly coal branches that it would be desirable that the government should acquire, as their usefulness as feeders of the government system justifies that acquirement. And, while this policy would measurably solve the transportation problems of the east, it would enable the people of the west to secure the full benefit and advantage of a government system of railways. For it is not only to the east but to the west as well that the Intercolonial is doing good-
What are you going to do with Prince Edward Island?

The government is dealing generously with Prince Edward Island. Only the other night we approved a resolution authorizing the governmnet to construct a branch line there. I am sure that my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) approves of that; and. if it is good policy for Prince Edward Island, it is good policy for the mainland as well.
But what about youi connecting link ? How are you going to make these Prince Edward Island roads feeders of the Intercolonial?

One thing at a time. If the hon. member will have a little patience he will find a tunnel built and a railway running under the straits. He wants everything in a moment. But he waited for generations-at least his political party did-without taking any step in that direction. The present administration are taking steps in that direction. And they are enlarging the railway system of Canada in every way. I invite the attention of the right hon. the First Minister to the subject I have mentioned, and would respectfully ask him, on behalf of the people of the ea3t particularly, whether the government have taken into consideration the acquirement of tlie branch lines connecting with the Intercolonial as feeders of the government railway system?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If there be those in this House who honestly believe that the time has come when public assistance to railway construction can be done away with, I do not share that opinion. On the contrary, our experience proves that the time, I am afraid, is very far distant in the future when we can in this country do as the United States has done, dispense with assisting by money grants the extension of our railway system to all parts of the country in which settlement has already gone. I have heard to-day voices from the province of Ontario and voices from the province of Quebec, protesting against any new subsidies towards railway construction. I venture *to say that if these voices had come from those parts of Canada in the condition they were forty years ago, they would have been the first to ask for railway subsidies. But I can conceive that some people in the province of Ontario and some portions of Quebec, where you have the country grid-ironed with railways, may think there is no necessity for a further advance in that direction. I would like hon. gentlemen who represent those, parts of Canada to remember that in the new provinces, In some parts of Ontario, in some parts of Quebec, and some other parts of the country, the conditions to-day are just as they were

forty years ago In Ontario, and if it were left to private enterprise to provide those sections with the blessings of railway transportation,, its is .probable that they would have to suffer a deprivation for many years to come. This policy was inaugurated many years ago, and so far as I can judge, and I think it is admitted by everybody, it has been a wise policy. It has done wonders for the country, and if the country is to-day as prosperous as it undoubtedly is, the fact is due to two causes, increased transportation and added immigration. As long therefore as immigration continues to flow in at the rate it is doing now, as long as the country settles up as rapidly as it is now being settled, I am afraid that no encouragement can be given to those who think that we can dispense with public assistance to railway transportation. We have done a good deal for the west, we are doing a good deal for the west in these resolutions. I confess that the west lias been usually well taken care of. My hon. friend for Westmoreland (Mr. Em-rnerson) asks if we are not going to do anything for the east. He has told us, not only this session but in preceding sessions, that the east is not as well provided for as it should be ; that at the present time there is.an anomalous condition of things prevailing, that is to say, that in all parts of the country where there are feeders to trunk lines these feeders are generally taken care of and put under the management of the trunk lines ; whereas in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick the feeders are not connected with the trunk lines. I believe that in this matter, and I think every body will agree with me, if the Intercolonial were under private management, all these feeders which are now merely branch lines would have been acquired by the company and would be part of the system at this moment.- But we must recognize that government management of a railway has not the elasticity which would as readily suggest of the adoption of such a policy. As long as there lacks such a union between the trunk lines and the feeders there must be an unsatisfactory condition of things to the people of the maritime provinces. On the other hand, we must recognize the fact that while the Idea is a good one, it involves very serious complications and requires serious consideration. I may say to my hon. friend, since he has put the question directly to me, that we have given very serious consideration to the condition of things which he has laid before us. While this condition of things is not a novel one, and we have given to it a good deal of consideration, we have not yet been able to make up our minds that it is a policy which we should adopt. Whilst we are not prepared to say to my hon. friend that we shall adopt this policy, we realize that it is one which requires consideration, and makes it incumbent upon the government to make the fullest inquiry in order that we may be in a position to discuss the matter adequately at another session.
Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on the resolutions.

Before this was drafted was there any arrangement made With these companies mentioned in this
section'

Just two companies to ibe known as the Canadian Northern. When ithey amalgamate, this guarantee of the bonds of this company takes effect, but we get a second mortgage on the entire system of the Canadian Northern Railway, including this part, which is to be part of the Canadian Northern Railway, and upon which we have a first mortgage. It is so worded as to guard that point by providing that the guarantee only becomes effective when this company and the Canadian Northern Railway are amalgamated into one-'new company, to be known as the Canadian Northern, each company carrying its own bonding powers into the new company.
If that new company is called the Canadian Northern, will there be any danger of mistakes being made? .
No, it will be the Canadian Northern Company.

But it will not be the Canadian Northern Company that exists
[DOT]to-day?
The Canadian Northern that exists to-day will be merged into this.

Do I understand the Minister of Railways and Canals to say that on the new part to be constructed you take a first mortgage, and that on the part lof the railway already ^constructed the Canadian Northern have the right of issuing securities to the amount of $20,000 a mile, which will be prior to the claim of the government, and that the government, for the sum of money which it advances on these new lines to be constructed, not only takes ,a first mortgage on the part to be constructed, but a second mortgage on the part constructed, and also gets the undertaking of the company for the repayment of the money?
Yes, they become the makers of the securities of the Canadian Northern Company.
In regard to the company that it is proposed to guarantee, all the obligations resting against them now will remain the same as heretofore, and the government's mortgage will be a second mortgage?
The government will have a first mortgage on all the lines not now constructed, but it will have a second mortgage over the entire Canadian Northern system on the lines already constructed.
Is not the Canadian Northern system subject to a second mortgage already?

I think not.
Mr. HAGGtART. I would like to know from my hon. friend what security we are going to get from the Canadian Northern, and what the pending liabilities are on this road on which we are taking a second mortgage.

If there be a second mortgage on the Canadian Northern, I must say it must be on a very small portion of it. My understanding of it was that our mortgage was over the entire system. I will get all the particulars when we rise at six. The main point is that this becomes part of the Canadian Northern system and carries with it all its properties and bonding privileges. The bonding privileges of the Edmonton, Yukon and Pacific Railway Company were changed not long ago. On the Mountain portion of the road, by the recent Act, they have bonding power to the extent of $3o,000 a mile and on the other portions of the road to the extent of $25,000 a mile.

Is this Edmonton, Yukon and Pacific Railway Company already chartered?
Mr. GR-AIIAM. Yes.

Who are the gentlemen composing the Edmonton, Yukon and Pacific Railway Company?
Mx-. GRAHAM. It is really the same interest as the Canadian Northern. That is why we are providing that the company must become the Canadian Northern.
Who are the gentlemen forming the company?
Mackenzie & Mann.
Have they the charter in their own name?

Yes. I happen to know that, as a positive fact, the shareholders and directors are Mackenzie & Mann and the gentlemen connected with them in the Canadian Northern system. They have built some fifty miles from Edmonton westward already.
