So eager are the people of the valley for the construction of this line that during the last session of the provincial legislature, the members upon both sides united in supporting the government proposal to guarantee the bonds of any railway company, which might become a part of a trunk line system, to the extent of $15,000 per mile. That idea was supported by all the members of the legislature on both sides and received general support among the people. As I understand the proposition of the gentlemen who, with Mr. Costigan, are promoting this charter and asking for this subsidy, is that they will carry their line from the Chaudiere Junction near Quebec, cross the international boundary and go through the state of Maine at its northern part, where it is comparatively narrow, instead of going up around the angle of the St. Francis river in the province of New Brunswick. It will cross the northern part of the state of Maine and connect there with a road down the St. John valley and make this road a part of the St. John valley system. I do not know whether that can be carried out; but I would say that if the line, as these gentlemen are proposing to have it constructed, is constructed to a point on the St. John in the vicinity of Grand Falls, it will give a great impetus to the construction of a line down the St. John valley. If it does not form part of such a through scheme, it will never be built because capitalists will not put their money into a local line. If built as a through scheme, it will be of enormous advantage to a country 290' miles in extent and one of the most fertile portions of Canada and which is to-day without the railway facilities enjoyed by most of the older sections of the Dominion.

I have listened patiently to the hon. minister. He has not said one word relating to the subsidy. He has given us a description of the country down about St. John at the other end of this line, but he might as well have told us how you would run the Transcontinental through British Columbia by describing a section of it in New Brunswick. This 62 miles is to run not from St. John to this point, but from the Chaudi6re at Quebec easterly.
Towards the St. John river.

But only as far as Kamour-aska. We are speaking only of 62 miles and not of all the way to St. John river. Your line may be an admirable way to reach the St. John valley, but there is no necessity for the Dominion bonusing 62 miles of road from the Chaudiere to the international boundary. Any gentleman who looks at the map will see that this line must run within two or three miles at the most from the Transcontinental, and it is not absurd to say that after building the Transcontinental, which could join with the line down to the St. John that my hon. friend speaks of, we should subsidize another line from the Chaudiere running alongside the Transcontinental for 62 miles.

The difficulty could be got over in this way. Suppose you give a subsidy to a line from the Chaudiere Junction to the state of Maine to connect with a road which connects with the St. Francis road running to Grand Falls down the St. Francis river, and then we will know the direction of this road. Instead of going around on the line of the Transcontinental, the parties evidently want to go to the state of Maine and make a short cut over to the line which they are at present constructing on the River St. Francis towards the Dominion.
For a line of railway from Tusket Wedge to a point on the Halifax Southwestern Railway at or near Riverdale station; not exceeding 8 miles.

This is a branch of the main line to Sussex village owned by the Halifax and Southwestern Railway Company.
To the Halifax and Southwestern Railway Company, for a line of railway from Lunenburg <to Bridgewater, via Upper Lahave; not exceeding 12 miles.

This is to connect Lunenburg with Bridgewater.
To the Erie, London and Tilsonburg Railway
Company, for a line of railway from _ Port Burwell to London, not exceeding 35 miles.

Knowing that district as well as I do, I would like to give the minister a little information. There is a railway already built from Port Burwell to Tilsonburg. ' Is it proposed to extend this into London ? Do they propose a new line from Port Burwell to London ? Port Burwell is sixteen miles from Port Stanley and there is a road from Port Stanley to London. Should there be a line between Port Burwell and London, these two lines will not be more than eight miles apart. That district is well supplied already with railway facilities by the Grand Trunk Railway, the Canada Southern and the Wabash line. The city of London and the county of Middlesex built a railway at their own expense many years ago, and I think it is hardly fair to

grant a bonus to a line which will be an opposition line to the London and Port Stanley Railway. If a company want to build a line to parallel that, they should be compelled to do it at their own expense. It is hardly fair to the city of London and the county of Middlesex, to have that line paralleled by another line bonused by this country. I hope the minister will look into the matter. The line from Port Burwell already built has been running for years into Ingersoll. The company were not able to run it, their cars were a disgrace, and they had to turn it over to the Canadian Pacific Railway to run it for them. To make an extension from Tilsonburg into London will simply parallel the London and Port Stanley Railway.
What distance from Tilsonburg to London ?

Some twenty-five miles. They are not going to build a line from Port Burwell to Tilsonburg when they have one built and one which they could not maintain and had to turn over to the Canadian Pacific Railway who are now running it. I do not want to move, but I call the attention of the minister and would like him to look into this matter before granting a bonus. ,

In raising the objection that this will give competition, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Beattie) does not agree with the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) who said that the main object of giving a subsidy was to bring competition.

The hon. minister is misrepresenting me. I said that the reason assigned in many instances for these subsidies was that they would be the means of building railways that would give competition, but sometimes these subsidized roads transferred their interests, perhaps to the very same railways w-itli which they were supposed to be competitors.

If there was any necessity for this road I would not say a word. Competition is well enough, but I do not see why the Dominion should help them to build another railway to compete with one built by the people of the locality with their own money.
On what ground is this subsidy granted?
The representations were as follows : The charter is from Port Burwell to London, with a branch to Tilsou-burg.
The line is already built from Port Burwell to Tilsonburg.
From Port Burwell to London, and London to Tilsonburg. But the proposed subsidy is from Port Burwell to London.
Tilsonburg comes in between.
That is not on the line.
Then you are going to run three lines eight miles apart.

The representation made to me by prominent men not connected with the road at all were that at present facilities are not afforded them to get in their coal supply which comes across the lake at that point. It is represented strongly, and the figures show, that if there was another road from Port Burwell to London with facilities for bringing coal across the lake that part of Western Ontario would save a large amount on the price of coal that must now come around by the bridge.

I am sorry that these prominent gentlemen have been deceiving the minister so badly. At Port Stanley we have had a car ferry that brings coal from Conneaut, and it has been running for years, long before they thought of having a car ferry at Port Burwell. The Grand Trunk, the Pere Marquette and other railways get their coal supplies in that way. The coal supply for London and district does not come by the bridge. As to building a branch railway from Port Burwell to London, the thing is a farce. Perhaps they might run a branch from Tilsonburg to London, but they are not going to build a railway to Port Burwell, a place with 25 inhabitants and no trade.

I am surprised to hear the manner in which the hon. member for London (Mr. Beattie) speaks of running a railway from Port Burwell to London by way of Tilsonburg. This railroad is intended to run from Port Burwell through the township of Malahide, through the town of Aylmer and Belmont into London. The charter was held for an electric railroad by a party living in Aylmer. Some years ago he asked for tenders for the construction of the road. I have been over the route. The holder of the charter was not able to finance the scheme. Since I became a member of the House another corporation have come to the House and got a charter for this road and propose to build the railway. Instead of being in opposition to the Port Stanley road, it will bring more trade into London. Port Stanley and Port Burwell are eighteen miles apart on the lake shore. From London to Port Stanley is twenty miles, from Port Stanley to Port Burwell eighteen miles and-
Sixteen miles, if you please.

And completing the triangle from Port Burwell to Aylmer is thirteen miles and from Aylmer to London through Belmont would make up the distance, 35 miles. It cannot be a competing road with the other, but would make a lot



of traffic tributary to London, besides giving the people of Port Burwell another outlet. If people wish to put money into a thing of this kind, if they come from the United States or England and put their money in and develop business, surely we should not object to that. It is enterprise such as this that has built London and all the other towns of this country.

I do not wish to take up the time of the committee, but I wish to say that the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. J. T. Schell) does not know what he jg talking about. Aylmer is twelve miles from St. Thomas. The existing road, with which this one, I contend, would compete, was built with the money of the city of London and Middlesex county, and the debt is about $2,000,000. These people propose to build a railway in opposition to that, when the road they have built to Tilson-burg could not be run-it was a disgrace to the country, running with a baggage car and an engine. It was handed over to the Canadian Pacific Railway who took it in order to get in their coal that way. But coal in cars has been brought across Lake Erie from Conneaut to Port Stanley long before a car ferry at Port Burwell was thought of. If the minister will look into the matter I shall be satisfied. I have no objection to the road being built, but I do not think the Dominion should give it a bonus.
For a line of railway from a point on the Canadian Pacific Railway at or near Plaster rock to Riley brook; not exceeding 28 miles.
Does this line to Plaster Rock run cars?
Yes.
Once a week, I suppose?
Daily. The Canadian Pacific Railway are operating it and doing it very successfully.

Making money.
To the Esquimalt and Nanaimo Railway Company, for a line of railway from a point near French creek to the village of Sandwich, not exceeding 11 miles; and for a line of railway from the village of Sandwich to Campbell river, not exceeding 38 miles; not exceeding in all 79 miles.
Does the Esquimalt and Nanaimo Railway ask for this?

Yes, they are giving a subsidy.
For a line of railway from a point at or near Cowley, in Alberta, to a point oin High-wood river; not exceeding 50 miles.
I move to insert at the beginning of the item : ' To the Southern Central Pacific Railway.'

I wish to say to the minister that I believe there are two charters over the same ground. The charter which is in existence is almost ready to expire, it has been in existence for a number of years, and there has been no work done. Another company has made application, but it has received no charter. It is ready to begin operations just as soon as they can get assistance ; perhaps they will without assistance. I think it is fair to say that if the new company is willing to build that road, it should get the same assistance, provided the old company is not going on.

This being the company that had the original charter, and the other company not having a charter, we thought the proper thing to do was to give the subsidy to the company having the old charter. If they do not make progress, we wfil be in a position to do something when it comes up again.
Is any portion of this road already built?
These are all small branches. I am told none of them are built.

None of these are built, but the main branch from Lake St. John road to La Tuque is built, some 25 miles, finished this spring. The main line is building these short branches. From the terminus of that line down to La Tuque none of them are built.
For a line of railway from Montreal to a point on the National Transcontinental Railway ; not exceeding 200 miles.

How is it that you give a subsidy for the purpose of connecting the National Transcontinental Railway with tho Northern Railway at Montreal when there is no subsidy to the Ontario people, who are building their own road? Why are they not as much entitled to it as the Quebec people?

There la a subsidy given to a company road to be built from Port

Arthur and Fort William to Sault Ste. Marie, about the same distance as this, and this is given to a company in Montreal. It has been the policy of the government not to give aid to the Ontario government railway.

That is what my hon. friend from Lanark refers to. He refers to the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway, the Ontario government road running north to North Bay. Is there anything in the subsidies for that road ? I understand that the Ontario government applied for a subsidy for that road.
I said it was not the policy of the Dominion government to aid the line of the Ontario government.
Why not?
That will open up a large question of policy.

The Quebec government may do this. This is for a line of railway, not to any particular company. They may make arrangements with the Quebec government to build it. You give it to the Quebec government, and you refuse the application of the Ontario government.
The Ontario government have not made any application.
You cannot give it to the Quebec government under this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This application was made some years ago by the late Quebec government, and it was not thought to be a wise policy at that time to assist local governments, if they wanted to build railroads, to come to the federal government for subsidies. The conclusion was reached several years ago when the application w7as made by the former government of Ontario.
I might call my hon. friend's attention to section 5 by which he will see that this subsidy must be given to a company.
The government are prepared to give substantial subsidies to connect cities in Quebec with the Transcontinental Railway, but when we reach Ontario they are not prepared to give a dollar.
Port Arthur is in Ontario.

It is not a city. The city of Toronto should be connected with the Transcontinental Railway in the same way as Montreal and Quebec are to be. Here is a subsidy given to one province for two hundred miles of railway to connect a great city with the Transcontinental Railway, but when you come into the province of Ontario it can get no subsidy. There is a discrimination in favour of one province as against the other.

Look at section 62.
422J

I am dealing with 49. It is enough at one time. That is the situation and that is something that will appeal to the people of Ontario as being unfair, because an application was made for a subsidy to assist in connecting the southern portion of Ontario and the city of Toronto with the Transcontinental Railway, and as far as we know, it was refused. At any rate, there was no assistance given, but in this case we give assistance towards the construction of two hundred miles of railway in the province of Quebec.
The Minister of Public Works drew my attention to clause 5. Does that provide that you cannot give a subsidy to a government?
It must be to a company or companies. The Governor in Council could not give a subsidy under this Act to any other than a company.

I would like to know from the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) the name of the company that is to get this subsidy for building two hundred miles of railway between Montreal and the Transcontinental Railway.

The name is not given here. As in a great many votes, the company is not named. My hon. friend will remember that a very large deputation from Montreal, perhaps as large a deputation, with the exception of that on the Georgian Bay canal, as any of those which have waited upon us this year, waited on the government some few weeks ago urging what, to my mind, was a very reasonable request, that there should be some provision made for connecting Montreal with the main line of the Transcontinental Railway. It was taken into consideration. Unless it be the Grand Trunk Pacific branch lines company I do not know what company would undertake this work. We do not name the company, but we will give the bonus to the company that will build this two hundred miles.

No individual without the authorization of the central legislative power can build a railway in this country under the present state of legislation. The company must be organized with power given to it by this parliament or a provincial legislature to build a railway and I would like to know if it is the intention of the government to grant that subsidy to the first company which is ready to build the branch line from Montreal to the Grand Trunk Pacific. Montreal has been waiting for four years for the building of such a railroad, that is already too much. In Montreal, we have been prevented from having anything to do with the building of the Transcontinental Railway though Montreal will pay more that any other city for such construction. I am quite ready to support this vote for the building of a branch^ line
13304

between Montreal and the Transcontinental Railway, but I would like to know if this subsidy is to be paid to any individual who is ready to organize a company to build the branch line or if it is to be paid to a company already organized. I would like to know if the Canada Central Railway Company or some other company I heard something about is to get this subsidy. Is it the policy of the government to pay over the subsidy to any individual or company who will first undertake and operate the construction of this branch line?
The policy of the government is to give the bonus to the first company that will show us that it is ready and aide to build a line connecting Montreal with the Transcontinental Railway.
Have conditions been laid down under which the subsidy can be earned?

There are the usual conditions. They have to make a contract with the Department of Railways and Canals which is approved by order in council. They will have to show their willingness, and, in our best judgment, their ability and we will make a contract with them to give them the subsidy for the building of that line.
Then the government is not already obliged to pay the subsidy except to a company which is ready to build and operate this railway according to law?
We are not committed to any person.
If I remember rightly the Ontario government are building their line of railway under the name of the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway Company.
No, not company; they are building it under the commissioners.
No. it is a company.

Not a company; it is a government owned road.
To the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, for branch lines of railway from the line of the National Transcontinental Railway to Port Arthur and Fort William; not exceeding 220 miles.
This is the province of Ontario.

Have you an agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to build this without any subsidy?
For a line of railway from Papineauvdlle on the Canadian Pacific Railway towards Nomin-ingue; not exceeding 30 miles.
This subsidy should read : To the Little Nation River Railway Company.

The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Major) points out that there Is Mr. GERYAIS.
a company organized hut that the minister did not get the application when the subsidy was decided on.
Has it .a charter ?
Yes.
Is it a Dominion or provincial charter ?
A provincial charter.
I thought it was not the policy of the government to subsidize provincial railways.
Tbat's a new idea.

That has been done for tlie last twenty years.
Resolution as amended agreed to.
Of the lines subsidized from No. 27 to No. 72 both Included, how many have already been constructed or partially constructed ?
I cannot tell without going through all these papers again.

On the second reading of the Bill and before committee, I will expect the hon. gentleman to give definite information on that point. I would like him to lay on the table also the applications from those several railway companies or corporations for the assistance now given.
I laid those on the table this morning.

They should be on the table for at least a week or ten days so that they may be examined by any one who desires. To put them on the table half an hour before the subsidies are taken up is not sufficient.
The mileage in operation and the mileage under construction will be found on the application forms.
I would like it stated on the second reading because it is a matter the minister should furnish to the committee without a suggestion by any member.
I did suggest it, in every application.

What is the use of talking of an application which was placed on the table of the House only to-day when every one was busy with the work of the
House, what is the use of speaking of that as information ?
I will look through the applications and secure the information.
Is not the proposed line from Quebec to Ottawa, that is the portion from Hawkesbury to Ottawa, almost constructed ?
A portion of that line is graded, there are no rails on it, no part of it is completed.
Was it commenced under any engagement from the government that it would be subsidized ?
None whatever, so far as I know.

In reference to the power of the government to give a subsidy to the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway Commission, let me quote from the Act constituting that body. It says :
The said board of commissioners shall be a body corporate under the name of the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Commission-
They have all the powers of a railway company, to work the road and everything else. It is provided here that the Governor in Council ' may grant subsidies to such companies as establish to the satisfaction of the Governor General.' This :s a body corporate and would come under this definition.
Is it not the property of the Crown ?
It is a body corporate and it does not matter to whom it belongs. You could change the wording to ' body corporate' if you chcse.
The minister might give us at a convenient time a statement showing how much of these subsidies and which of them will go to each of the three large railways in Canada.

I shall try tc do that, it is not sometimes easy as they are sometimes lor a large company although under another name.
To the Canadian Pacific Railway Company (lessees of the Calgary and Edmonton Railway Company), towards the construction and completion of a bridge over the Saskatchewan river connecting Sfcrathcoma and Edmonton, 15 per cent upon the amount expended thereon; not exceeding $100,000.

Has the minister taken any steps to make this a combination wagon and railway bridge which it readily conceded to be advisable to do with such bridges ?
Mi'. GRAHAM. The government has not
taken any steps in that direction, but I understand some arrangement has been made between the provincial authorities and the company to provide for traffic on this bridge.
I see there is provision for that in one of the Quebec bridges and it would seem to be equally good policy iu Alberta.

Of course in the Northwest this government has charge of
the land and the provinces have not land to sell as in the east to raise money to build bridges. At Port Saskatchewan the government required the Canadian Northern Northern Railway to have a traffic bridge and it is a perfect boon to the place.
To the Quebec, Montreal and Southern Railway Company, towards the construction and completion of -the following railway bridges:
(a)	bridge across the Gentilly river, $15,000.
(b)	bridge across the Beoamcourt river, $30,000.
(c)	bridge across the Richelieu river, $30,000.
What are these bridges supposed to cost ? We are giving lump sums for small bridges and it seems doubtful policy.

The bridges are in the county of Nico'et which I represented at the beginning of this parliament. These are large rivers and this represents about 15 per cent of the cost of the bridges. The railway is the Quebec, Montreal and Southern, but although it is operated under that name I think the company has transferred its interest to the Delaware and Hudson which will run now from the boundary line to Quebec on the south shore, the railway nearest to the St. Lawrence. It has practically built from Montreal to Ste Philom&ne iu the county of Lotbiniere and is going on with the construction from Ste. Philo-niene to LGvis It is a first-class road doing its work extremely well, and as I said this represents about 15 per cent of the cost.
That bridge across the Richelieu is an old friend of ours.

My hon. friend is referring to the Yamaska river. This bridge is
on the Richelieu.
To the Atlantic, Quebec and Western Railway Company, towards the construction and completion of the twenty-six railway bridges on its line of railway from P&spebiac to Gaspe, payable upon the completion of the said line of railway between the said points, $250,000.

This' is in my constituency. It Is a very exceptional case. For many years past the peninsula of Gasp6 has been clamouring for the construction of a railway to Gaspe from New Carlisle, the terminus of the Atlantic and Lake Superior. One hundred miles is built between Meta-pedia and New Carlisle. In 1903 I secured a charter for this railway from New Carlisle to Gaspg Baffin, about 102 miles. The new company has built 20 miles which are in operation and 20 miles further will be in operation the 1st November next. It is a very rugged section of country. They were obliged to follow the shore and cross twenty-five rivers from PasJJebiac to Gaspe Basin. They obtained the ordinary subsidy, but with these twenty-six bridges they were entitled to a special subsidy. This will insure the construction of the line in about

twelve months from now. There is a tunnel also of 230 feet which they have to build.

This is a strange way of subsidizing bridges. We take a whole line of railway, we do not know what the bridges are going to cost, some of them may not be very costly, they may be only small bridges crossing small streams, there may be others larger, but we count up all the bridges on a line of railway 200 miles long and we give the company $250,000. We subsidize in one breath twenty-six bridges without knowing whether they are expensive or inexpensive to build. In other cases when applications are made for subsidies to build bridges, each bridge is considered on its individual merits but not so in this matter. How do we know how many of these bridges come within the principle we have laid down which justifies our subsidizing bridges at all?
There are twenty-six bridges. One was built since the line was started.
Was that subsidized ?

Not specially, only the ordinary subsidy. If we followed the ordinary principle of allowing 15 per cent on the cost of construction, four bridges alone would take the amount mentioned in the resolution, $250,000-the bridges across the St. John river, the Grand river, the Pabos and Little river. If you take the cost of construction of those four bridges alone, the 15 per cent on that would amount to the $250,000 now granted.
On those four large bridges the Quebec government also promised a subsidy, provided they would be made suitable for vehicles to cross. That condition is attached by the Quebec government to the special subsidy they are giving. This is a section of country where railway construction is badly needed and where the company have shown good reason why the government should help them, because with the ordinary subsidy they have gone to work and built an excellent line some twenty miles long and twenty more will be built by the 1st November next, and by the 1st November the year following the whole line will be in operation.
I suppose this line of railway is subsidized.
The ordinary subsidy.

We are establishing a dangerous precedent. Every one of these railway companies will consider itself warranted in coming back to the government and saying: Treat us as you have done the Atlantic, Quebec and Western Railway Company. You have subsidized our railway line first, and now you should subsidize our bridges. Give us proportionately the same assistance for the erection of these bridges 1 Mr. LEMIEUX.
that you gave the other railway company. The government are establishing a bad precedent which will give trouble in the future.

Let me show my hon. friend what the company is accomplishing which entitles it to a special subsidy. This company was subsidized to build a railway from Paspebiac to Gaspe basin and thence a railway through the interior, from Gaspe basin to Causapscal in the county of Bona-venture. In order to obtain this special subsidy for bridges, it has abandoned the subsidies allowed for that line from GaspS basin to Causapscal because the government could not grant a subsidy on that interior line plus the $250,000 for bridges. As the settled parts of the country have to be served before the wilderness, the company have abandoned the construction of the line through the interior for the time being, although their charter still holds good.

That does not touch the point I raised. You first subsidize the railway and then you take all the bridges in a group and subsidize them to the tune of a quarter of a million dollars. This will establish a very bad precedent. Other railway companies with equal propriety, can come and ask that the same thing be done for them.

I can assure my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) that in the whole list of railways that are subsidized especially for bridges, there is no case identical with this. There are twenty-six bridges of which at least four are very large bridges and going to cost more than a million on a line of about a hundred miles. There is not a similar case in the whole railway construction of Canada.

When we grant a round sum per mile for a railway, does not that include the bridges ? If you pay $15,000 a mile, that is for the whole railway, bridges and everything else.
To the Interprovincial Railway Bridge Company of New Brunswick, towards the construction and completion of a railway bridge over the Restngouche river from Campbellton to Mission point, $160,000.
What is that bridge to cost ?

Between $050,000 and $750,000. The Deputy Minister of Railways reports something over $650,000.
To the Vancouver, Westminster and Yukon Railway Company, .towards the construction and completion of a railway bridge across Burrard inlet, $200,000.
What will be the cost of this bridge ?

This partially answers the Question asked of the hon.^ member for East Hamilton (Mr. Barker)-if you subsidize the railway does not that include the bridges ? This says :
Unless the context otherwise requires, the expression ' oost ' me tuns the actual, necessary and reasonable cost, and shall include the amount expended upon any .bridge up to .and not exceeding $25,000.
So, you first subsidize the railway at $3,200 a mile, or more if the expense of construction calls for it, this subsidy including the bridges, and then you subsidize the bridges again.

No doubt, special cases are made by the government to meet special conditions. Some years ago the policy seems to have been adopted of paying 15 per cent on a bridge, and that seems to be about the usual percentage paid on these large bridges. But special cases are made out year after year.
These other sections are without change ?
They are taken word for word from the existing statute.
What is meant by the completion of a subsidized railway ? Does it mean that the railway is absolutely com-nleted and ready for the running of trains ?

1 believe that sometimes subsidies are given on 10-mile sections. The road must be completed up to a certain standard and examined by the engineer of the department. He gives his certificate that the road Is so constructed and we pay on that.

I have been asking with regard to a portion of the Canadian Northern between Erwood and the Pas Mission on which a subsidy of land Is given. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) promised to give me the report of the engineer who visited the line. He gave me one this morning, but it is not the one I referred to. This was made in February when the railway was under a foot of snow. I would ask the minister if he cannot bring down the report of the engineer sent to inspect the line last fall.
The report I gave the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lake) is the only one I know of.
Another Inspection was made. The engineer told me he had been over the line and gave me a graphic description of it. I think that was in October. No doubt he made a report, and that is what 1 wanted.
I will look into it and see if there is another report. When I came across this one X thought it was the one the hon. gentleman wished to see.

(Translation.) I propose :
That paragraph 4 he amended by adding after subsection (d) the following additional subsection as subsection (e):
Henceforth, ho such subsidy shall be paid for any railway to any railway company, unless such company or companies provide for a proper and gratuitous roadway for vehicles as well as for foot-passengers on those bridges, the plans and specifications for such construction to be submitted to the Governor in Council, for approbation.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak at any length, ,1 think the time has come when the government should Inaugurate a new railway policy. This evening, we have voted over five hundred thousand dollars in aid to the construction of railway bridges. Why not provide that railway companies shall build those bridges in such a way as to afford a roadway for foot passengers and for vehicles? Have not those companies received large enough subsidies from the public exchequer, and consequently are we not entitled to stipulate in return those advantages in favour of the public? I do not wish to add anything further on the question, but it seems to me that it is sufficient to call the attention of the government to the matter to induce them to make the change asked for. I have no doubt that my proposal will meet with a favourable reception at the hands of the government.

There are two difficulties. First, my hon. friend moves an amendment that no subsidy shall be paid for these railway bridges unless they place a gratuitous passage way for vehicles as well as foot passengers. Does not my bon. friend see that four out of five of these bridges will be where there are no roads, and possibly no foot passengers ? You would not want a roadway for vehicles where there is no roadway.

As soon as the bridge is built the road would be constructed to the bridge. If the company are obliged to build a passage way for vehicles, they can build it cheaper when they are building the bridge in the first place, than if they add the passage way afterwards. It will cost them twice as much to add the passageway as it would to build it with the bridge 'in the beginning.

I am not forgetting that engineering point. What my hon. friend says about cheapness will not always work out. I bad the engineers on that problem the other day, and I found that a bridge could be built with a roadway much cheaper than a roadway could be added to a railway bridge. But that difficulty does exist in some places. No doubt a roadway over a bridge would be very convenient and altogether desirable. But I make the

statement again, that in at least seventy-five per cent of the railway bridges of Canada, there would he no need for a roadway for foot passengers, because the bridges are away from a road altogether. Then there is the other objection. It is a fair and reasonable objection that the Dominiou government cannot well undertake to start in providing roadways. That is purely a municipal or a provincial affair. While I would be delighted to see them on every bridge, still it is a matter with which the province alone ought to deal with the corporation.

I think my hon. friend from Laval (Mr. Leonard) has made a most important suggestion, and I had hoped that the government would adopt it. We are paying-I am speaking now principally for the province of Quebec-large subsidies for bridges for companies which, in the majority of cases, are well able to build those bridges themselves without any government assistance at all. Speaking specially of grants in the province of Quebec, I doubt very much if the percentage exists mentioned by the Postmaster General. I think the amount we are granting to villages, particularly on the south shore of the St. Lawrence, is a much larger percentage of the cost of these bridges. There is here an opportunity for the government to render a great service to people along the line of these railways. What are the objections ? They are futile. The Minister of Railways says there are no roads where most of these bridges are built. The answer of my hon. friend from Laval is that as soon as that condition is performed there will be no road to these bridges. Just as soon as roadways were built on the Victoria bridge in Montreal, when that bridge was changed, a magnificent roadway was built up to it. The other objection of the minister is that we have no jurisdiction oven roads in municipalities and over bridges in the provinces. That seems to me to be an objection equally futile, because whether we have jurisdiction or not, we are not assuming to exercise jurisdiction. We are imposing a condition on a grant of money, and we can impose any condition we like. There is no question of jurisdiction. A case has been pointed out to me by my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) of a subsidy granted for a bridge over the river Jacques Cartier in the province of Quebec, conditional on the company constructing a bridge for vehicular traffic. In most cases the municipalities are not in a position to build suitable bridges, in most cases the provinces are not in a position financially to come to the assistance of the municipality. These subsidies are extremely generous, and I think the government ought to accept this condition. There is another point. This afternoon, in Mr. GRAHAM.
the space of four hours, we have been granting nearly $20,000,000 of money without giving those grants the consideration they require. It seems to me to be most absurd, to pass these grants with the little consideration we are giving them, it is perfectly ridiculous. I think the time has arrived when we should adopt for our own preservation some rule by which resolutions of this kind must be brought before the House at least one month before prorogation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The suggestion of the hon. gentleman is important and in a sense it would be valuable, but much more valuable if it were addressed to provincial and municipal authority. It is simply a proposal to unload on the Dominion treasury the obligations of the provincial government and the municipal authorities. There may be exceptional instances in which .while constructing a bridge, we might be able at the same time to construct a highway. But if we are to lay down a principle that this government must provide highway bridges of that kind, I certainly think my hon. friend is mistaken in putting such a project before the House. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) says that the municipalities are not usually able. Well, I question whether he is justified in making that statement, I think most municipalities are able. He says that the provincial governments are not able to do this. I must dissent entirely. Our provincial governments are not so poor that they are not able to provide highways for the people of their respective provinces. They have certainly received large additions to their subsidies, and I think they are well able to perform the duties which under the circumstances, are assigned to them.
We are not in Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, while I would not undertake to make any analysis of the financial affairs of the province of Quebec, I understand that they are regarded as being in a satisfactory condition. But I am dealing now with the principle. In the case of a municipal or a provincial work it is proposed to say that this work shall be constructed at the expense of the Dominion government.
Why was that condition imposed when a subsidy was given to the Victoria bridge ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot recall the circumstances. There may be exceptional circumstances in all these matters. But the effect of the motion of my hon. friend is to unload upon the Dominion treasury obligations which really belong to the municipal and provincial authorities. We may have done it in some cases, and i.t may be

open to objection, bnt that is no justification for laying down the principle that we are going to do it all the time.

It does not seem to me that this is unloading anything on the Dominion treasury. It is unloading something upon these companies. It may be, as the Minister of Railways has said, that it would not be practicable, in all cases. Certainly it is practicable in a great many other cases, as it has been carried out in the case of the Intel-provincial bridge at Ottawa, Victoria bridge at Montreal and many others.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the province contributed, but I am not sure.

It may be so. I am not aware that the province contributed to the cost of the Victoria bridge at Montreal, but I think my hon. friend is quite right in saying that either one or both of the provinces contributed to the cost of the Interprovincial bridge at Ottawa. The Dominion government gave a subsidy to this bridge, but the provincial government gave a subsidy also, and a footway may have been a condition of the subsidy of one or either of the provincial governments. That is not true of the Victoria bridge, and I think it is not true in some other cases. The proposition of my hon. friend from Laval (Mr. Leonard) does not in the slightest degree impose any further demand on the Dominion treasury.

Does not my hon. friend see that if you make it a provision that they must have a roadway on all these bridges the applicants will ask for more subsidy? If the Dominion gives a subsidy without making any provision for a roadway, and then imposes that condition, the company receiving the subsidy will ask for more. If you give $?5,000, and afterwards put in a condition that will make the work cost $10,000 more, they will need $35,000 to enable them to construct the bridge. You will have municipal councils coming here whenever they want a bridge to be built, and you will have provincial governments also asking aid towards the construction of bridges. My hon. friend points out conditions that may arise, but there is nothing to prevent us from aiding the construction of a bridge, but to say that the Dominion government must provide a roadway on every bridge that is constructed is to suggest something that any railway man who is building bridges will tell you is not practicable.

These bridges that tire going to be built in Quebec-I suppose the conditions are the same everywhere

were intended to be built whether there was a subsidy or not. My hon. friend the Postmaster General knows perfectly well that this railway, which goes from St. Lambert to Levis, is being built by a well known
American company, it is partly built now, it is under process of construction, one of the finest roads on the continent, and they intended building those bridges anyway without any doubt. They are able to do it. We come to their assistance and give them quite considerable subsidies in aid of the bridges over the rivers which the line crosses between St. Lambert and Lfivis. It is a perfectly suitable condition to impose that the bridges should be built according to certain plans and to say that they must have our approval. Impose this additional condition while the bridge is being built. It scarcely adds to the cost of the bridge, and will be an immense boon to the whole population. I hope the government will see fit to adopt the amendment of my hon. friend from Laval.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I illustrate what I think is the correct principle by a reference to what was done in the case of an important bridge in Prince Edward Island? The government built a bridge in Prince Edward Island as a portion of the Prince Edward Island Railway, known as the Hillsborough bridge. In that case the provincial government wanted a highway, but this government obliged the provincial authorities to pay their fair share towards that highway, and we deduct every year from the subsidy to Prince Edward Island a certain sum of money ; I think it is $12,000.
How much did it cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A large sum of money.
A very large sum of money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A very large sum of money. We said to the provincial government : We will build a bridge for railway purposes, because that is the proper function of the Dominion government, but we will not build a bridge for highway purposes. That is your proper function. Prince Edward Island is not as rich as Ontario or Quebec. Prince Edward Island is not too flourishing, but so fair and reasonable was that proposal that the Prince Edward Island government accepted the responsibility, and every year there is a sum deducted from their subsidy to pay the provincial obligation for providing a provincial highway. This proposal is that while we do that with Prince Edward Island we are going to oblige the Dominion government, out of its treasury, to provide highways in some other provinces.

The case of the Hillsborough bridge was quite exceptional. It was a matter of negotiation for a long time between the provincial and Dominion governments. It is questionable whether we should have gone into that expense, but, at any rate, the circumstances are altogether exceptional.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will venture to say that if we should adopt my hon. friend's principle you would have the Prince Edward Island government here speedily asking for a refund of the money.
Amendment (Mr. Leonard) negatived.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is very important. The French version is absolutely as much law as the English, and if a man is being tried for his life in the province of Quebec it might depend upon the exact meaning of the word which is used in the French version so that if a wrong word is used it might have serious consequences.

The Minister of Justice misapprehends the remark of my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule). For the very reason that it is important he pointed out that such mistakes as these in the French version should not occur. It is undoubtedly of the highest importance that the French version should be correct, and for that reason my hon. friend pointed out that greater care should be taken.

1 would agree with the leader of the opposition if we were discussing the translation of a literary work, but the whole inspiration of our criminal Code comes from the English law and when you come to translate the English law into French you meet with serious difficulties. I studied the criminal law at Laval under Mr. Justice Delorimier and in many instances he had to use the English text to give the exact meaning of the law. It is a most difficult thing and it is not surprising that here and there in the Criminal Code we should meet some expressions which do not convey the exact meaning of the original English text. We come immediately after this clause upon the word ' robbery ' in English. You have the word ' robbery ' and the word * theft.' In French we have only the word ' vol.' There is in each of these English words a nuance, as we say in French, which is very difficult to express; we have to use several words to express the English meaning. It i3 very difficult to translate the English criminal law into French exactly.

Which makes it all the more apparent that we should have had the French version prepared and passed through parliament at the same time as the English, instead of leaving it to be prepared months afterwards against the remonstrance of gentlemen on both sides of the House. The present difficulty seems to arise largely from the course which was then adopted. Hon. gentlemen protested that the two versions should be concurrent, that they are of equal validity throughout the country and therefore that we should not have one presented and the other handed in at a later stage. However, there is no doubt about the importance of the amendment.

haul ' in the third line the words ' i i a l'in-tention de porter a une personne des coups ou blessures qu'il sait etre de nature a causer la mort/ and by substituting ' erreur ' for ' mal-adresse ' in the same line.

It Is remarkable that we should have the amendment of the section presented in an entirely defective form according to the view of the Postmaster General, after it has been prepared by the Justice Department.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There Is nothing extraordinary about what has taken place, if hon. gentlemen will reflect what the circumstances are. We are putting into the French language English terms of art with reference to the criminal law. There are fine shades of meaning in the words which are used in describing offences in the English law. The word in question is 'robbery.' Every lawyer who practises the English law understands the difference between robbery and theft or stealing or simple larceny. That is not so easy a difference to define in the French language. The

omission of these words has been by some accident and was called to my attention by Mr. Justice Cross who noticed in trying a case that in this very Important section these four words had somehow been omitted. I do not know whose fault it was, it might have occurred through a printer's error or in the preparation of the manuscript, but it being necessary to supply the words which have been dropped the question arises what word are you to use as the French equivalent for robbery. The natural word is the word used, ' vol,' but that means theft, larceny, a trifling stealing. A man may be guilty of murder constructively, so to speak, by killing another while engaged in burglary or robbery, although he did not intend to kill. But if a man is engaged in some little theft, stealing a chicken, for instance, it would not involve such serious consequences. For that reason after discussing the matter with the Postmaster General, I suggested that an amendment should be made.

The minister sayS there is nothing extraordinary about this and there is not, having regard to our experience. We have already had numerous amendments to these revised statutes, which must be cut and hacked and slashed now to an extraordinary extent. Putting through the English version without the French is probably one of the causes for this difficulty.

Is any compensation to be allowed the relatives of Captain Arthur Clark, who was killed by the explosion of a gas buoy at Parry Sound ?

I do not remember with certainty, but I think that Captain Clark's heirs have made application for a petition of right. We maintain that the accident was due entirely to the negligence of Captain Clark and that, under the circumstances, we would not be liable.
He left a widowed mother who had been dependent upon him for support. I understand there is a claim before the department, and I had hoped that the minister would have done something for her.	*

If I remember the circumstances, the accident was due to his own negligence. He left the buoys in the ice instead of putting them in a dry place, and iwhen he went there in the spring to lay them up the accident occurred.
Still, he was in the employ of the government, and I see that other allowances are made-for instance, there is a compassionate allowance to the heirs of a ma.n who was killed.

He was not in the employ of the government but was under contract.
AD1. BENNETT. But the buoys were supplied by the department, and if there was anything defective in them, allowance should be made. Allowance was made for the explosion at Kingston, I believe.
The explosion at Parry Sound was not due to a defect in the buoy. Captain Clark left it in the water, and it was as a result of that that the explosion occurred.
Will the minister grant a petition of right ?
Oh. yes. I will not offer any obiection so long as the Alinister of Justice is agreeable.

I think with my hon. friend from Simeoe that most accidents occur through the negligence of the men themselves, still I do not think that ought to be set up as a reason why the government should not consider a claim. I am speaking in a general way. I do not think that because an accident happens to a man while he is in the employ of the government or any one else, and it happens in consequence of his own carelessness, that that should be a reason altogether why his family should be deprived of a gratuity.

There may be some difference due to the fact that he was not in the employ of the government, but he was performing a contract with the government in placing these buoys. In the fall of the year he went up there to collect these buoys, and instead of putting them in a dry place left them in the water. When he went up there to float them the accident occurred.
All-. BENN'ETT. I hope the minister will reconsider the case and do something in the matter.

It was stated by the hon. gentleman's predecessor that there was something to be known which would account for these explosions, which they did not know. But several of them have occurred within a few years, and no reasonable explanation was given the House why they happened. I take it that this is on a par with the others.

These young men may not have known that the buoys were dangerous if left out in a damp place, and that may not have been explained to them. If that was the case here, I think the government should reconsider.
I did not like to take the resjionsibility of paying the money. The claim was a very large one, and I thought it would be better to refer the matter to the courts.
Alake them an offer of some kind and see if they will accept it.
Is it in the courts now ?
They were told that we would grant a petition of right, and my impression is that they have made application for a petition of right. If they have, it has been granted.
Perhaps they cannot afford to pay the costs.

I do not think that sufficient precaution was taken to inform these men, who are not accustomed to these buoys, that they were dangerous to handle. A serious accident nearly happened with a gas buoy in my district and it was only by a miracle that two or three were not killed. A man who is a thoroughly competent engineer nearly lost his arm and his eyesight. I think the minister

ought to see that men who handle these gas buoys are cautioned as to their danger.

The new gas buoys that we are adopting do not offer any danger at all. In the accident that happened at Kingston, and th*f which happened to Captain Clark, the buoys were high pressure gas buoys. The gas was made on shore and transferred by a tender to the gas buoys, which were charged with it. It was a dangerous thing. These gas buoys had a pressure of, I think, in some cases, 150 atmospheres. But with the new system of gas buoys, what we call the Willson gas buoys, there is very little danger, because they are worked under an automatic system, that is to say, we simply take the carbide and put it in the buoy and gas is produced automatically. They have only a pressure of five atmospheres. So there is much less danger.

Will he say that it is not working towards the member's wharf?
I could not say.
There is a boat house there, is there not?
I do not know.
Is it built on the property of the member ?
Not knowing whether there is a boathouse there or not, I could not say.

Very well.
Suimtnerside harbour breakwater-additional revote, $19,000, $25,000.
Mr. FOWLER, How much are you going to spend there?
About $133,000, that is the contract.
New Brunswick-Beaver harbour wharf. $5,000.
This is new?
Yes.
Is it under contract?

It will be. Plans are not prepared.
Gampbellton deep water wharf-extension repairs, &c., additional amount, $10,000.
Will that complete the work?

I think so. It is under contract.
Dorchester wharf-addition to, additional amount, $7,000.
What are you doing there?

Building an addition to the wharf, making It suitable for large steamers. Quite a large lumber business is done there.	[DOT]
Harvey bank wharf, $5,000.
What is to be built there?
There are two sites offered, one where the wharf will cost $12,000 and one where it can be built for $6,600. I think the one at $6,600 will be sufficient.
You have not .yet purchased the site?	[DOT]

No.
Larneville breakwater wharf, $8,000.
Is that under contract ?

It will he.
Leonards vi lie, Deer island-reconstruction and extension of wharf, $4,500.
What Is to be the total cost ?

About $4,500.
Miadawaska river-extension of dyke on east side of river at Edimundiston and repairs to a portion of dyke damaged by fire in September, 1907-(additional amount, $3,000.
Will this complete the work ?
Yes.
What will be the total ?

About $13,000.
Misoou-extension of wharf, $4,000.
That is in Gloucester too?.
Yes.
Will this $4,000 cover the cost ?
The chief engineer thinks so.
What is the need of that extension ?
To get a greater depth of water to accommodate larger vessels. The tendency is for larger vessels to use this wharf.

Large steamers come to this point from Halifax, and this is to enable them to reach the wharf.
New Mills wharf, $5,000.
Is that quite new ?
Yes.
Will this be the total cost ?
No.
What is the estimate?

Probably $15,000. The
contract is not let yet.
St. John river and tributaries-construction of wharfs in tidail waters, $15,000.

I propose out of this to commence the construction of several wharfs which are urgently required. Among others, one at Oromocto, a high water wharf, costing about $6,000 ; one at Burton, estimated at $3,000 ; one at Sheffield, estimated at $1,500 ; one at Mauger-ville. One is required at Barker's, one at Scotch Town, one at Newcastle, one at Lower Gage Town, one or two on the Ken-nebecasis, including Rothesay. Then there are one or two urgently required in the parish of Westfield. My idea was that by the time the engineer gets the plans and specifications ready and tenders are called for, probably the amount I am asking for will enable me to begin the construction of these various wharfs the present year.
I would like to put in a word for a high water wharf at Brown's Flats, which is very much required.

That is under consideration. In addition to the $15,000, I have an amount in the main estimates to pay one-half the cost of construction of certain other works, with tile idea that the provincial government will pay one-half.
I notice that the minister has put in a great deal of this money for works in the upper part of the St. John.
There are a good many wharfs already built in the lower part. They are kept in pretty good repair by the provincial government.

That high water wharf at Brown's Flats is more urgently required than any you have mentioned.
St. John river-to ma ke survey 1m'tween Fredericton and Woodstock with a view of improving navigation, $5,000.
What does the minister propose to do with reference to this survey?
When the estimate is passed I shall ask the chief engineer to organize an engineering party to engage at once in the work of making a survey.
Is it proposed to spend $5,000 for the purpose of surveying the river channel between Fredericton and Woodstock in order to ascertain where dredging is required?
It is proposed to expend that if it is necessary.

I want to say that I regard this appropriation as a most ridiculous one. It is absolutely unnecessary for the purpose. There are six or seven places on the St. John river between Fredericton and Woodstock where dredging is necessary. These points are just as well known to men who are familiar with the river as the villages and post offices along the river. What the people of Fredericton and York county who are interested in navigation want is not $5,000 frittered away in an unnecessary and useless survey of this kind, but they want the channel cleared and dredged. They want some work done this season. If the minister, instead of asking for $5,000, had asked for double that amount and sent a dredge up to do the work, he would have acted more in accordance with the requirements of the situation. This matter had been standing for two or three years, neglected by this government, so that the result was that the people of the St. John valley have now lost the only means of communication they had between Woodstock and Fredericton. To propose now a survey of the river between these points and organize a surveying party for the purpose is the height of absurdity. Last year I called the attention of the acting Minister of Public Works to this matter. I had ascertained myself, from well known river men, at what points dredging w.as necessary, and I sent a memorandum to the Department of Public Works. If the minister will write to the resident engineer of St. John, I will venture ito say that he will find out by means of a letter or two just where dredging is necessary, and if he had the interests of the people of the River St. John at heart he would consider it his duty to start that work without delay instead of wasting money in such a survey as he proposes. I will give the minister a pointer, that if he wants to get any votes at all for his candidate along the St. John river in the coming election, he had better not start any ' more surveys in that district. The people of the St. John river have had enough of election surveys. They had a survey prior to the last election which cost thousands and thousands of dollars, which was abso-

lutely a fake survey conducted for no other purpose than deceiving the people on the eve of the election. I could quote the words of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), that this was a survey which could not be depended upon. He denounced it in the Liberal convention in St. John as a survey which was no survey at all, of which there was not even profiles. If the minister wishes his friend Mr. Whitehead to get any votes at all along the St. John river, he had better not try the survey business on the people there again.

If I thought I knew as much about this matter as the hon. gentleman thinks he knows, but about which he does not know anything perhaps, I would be prepared to express my opinion on the question of engineering as to what is necessary to improve navigation on the St. John river. The problem is not such an easy one as the hon. gentleman seems to think. It is a problem which requires considerable engineering skill and I would not have thought that I would have been justified in asking for an appropriation from this parliament to engage upon the work of improving the navigation of the River St. John between Fredericton and Woodstock before first having had a proper survey made to determine the cost of the work and to find out what the result would be. The hon. gentleman says you have just to go and do some dredging. There is an engineer's report in my department which says that there is one place alone at Bear island where it will he necessary to construct a wing dam which will probably cost from $20,000 to. $25,000 and there are probably other places along the St. John river where the same thing would be necessary.
How long has that report been on file in the department in regard to Bear island ?
For some little time; I do not know how long it has been there. It is a report which has been made by a competent engineer.	-
By Mr. Shewen ?
I think by Mr. Shewen, who is a very competent engineer indeed.
And jou want a survey to verify the report ?

I want a survey of the whole river between Fredericton and Woodstock for the purpose of ascertaining what the work is going to cost and whether, when the work has been done it will result in the improvement of the navigation of the river. I am not going to be rushed into an expenditure even in my own province until I am satisfied by the opinion of engineers that the expenditure will be profitable and will result in the improvement of navigation.
How long does the minister expect this survey to continue ?	.
As long as is necessary.
Will it be completed during the present season of navigation ?
Just as quickly as is reasonably possible.

Does the minister expect it will be completed during the present
season ?
I hope it will.

It is a great satisfaction to know as much as the hon. member for York (Mr. Crocket) does but, unfortunately, there are a few people in Canada who are not in that happy condition. This survey is the result of a joint meeting of a number of people in his own constituency, in Carle-ton and the board of trade of Woodstock, who are interested in the question of having steamer navigation on the River St. John. The meeting was held in Woodstock in May. I received a resolution passed at that meeting and I presume my hon. friend did the same. [DOT]

I brought this matter up two years ago. I pointed out to the hon. member for Carleton himself that Woodstock was as much interested in this as the people of York, and asked him, to support me in my demand, and not till then was the hon. gentleman heard from in the matter.

I admit that. I am only pointing out to my hon. friend who makes so light of the fact of a survey being undertaken why I am asking for it and I admit that I have asked the minister to make this survey. It is because a number of people interested in it passed a resolution at a formal meeting attended by a hundred people in Woodstock asking that this survey be made. These gentlemen intend to put money into a steamer if something is done to make the project feasible, they do not know all about it and they have asked for this survey. I transmitted this memorial to the Minister of Public Works and I asked that he put an amount in the supplementary estimates in order that this survey might be made. This survey will be made. I am not perhaps as optimistic as to the results of dredging this river as the hon. member for York is, but I hope that they will be such as will justify the expenditure of some money and that the work will result in the improvement of navigation.

With regard to what my hon. friend from Carleton has said, the answer, I think, will be found in a speech which "he made in this House the other night in which he said that there were six

or seven points between Fredericton and Woodstock where dredging was required. That is the same statement that was forwarded to the department by myself last year. He said that with the exception of these points the channel would be clear and that dredging would be required only at these .places. He asked that the dredging be done this season, and suggested that if that couid not be done a survey might be made. That did not look as if at that time he felt very strongly that any survey was necessary.
Tracadie-works for protection of channel and lighthouse, $2,500.
Is that not in Gloucester county ?
Yes.
What do you want done there ?
It is for the protection of the channel and lighthouse.

At Tracadie there is an exportation of lumber to the amount of from 16,000,000 to 18,000,000 feet every year. The Snowball Company themselves cut about 8,000,000 feet.
Mr. FOWLER, This is for the Snowballs?
The Tracadie Lumber Company do a large business and the Arsenaults and Fergusons ship from there and many others also.
What will be the cost and what will be the result of this work?
The cost is estimated at $2,500.
What is this for?

The harbour commissioners have urged us to build a wharf for the increasing business. I hesitated somewhat about it though I was impressed with the necessity for it and when the fire'occurred I thought it would be better to build it this year.
Is it for a private coal dealer?

No, public business.
Goderich harbour - breakwater-additional amount, $228,000.
What did that breakwater cost altogether?
Goderich harbour-to pay claims of Smeeth & McGillicuddy in connection with construction of wharf, $4,205.93.
Was that settled by arbitration?

The work was done under the direction of Mr. Gray who is now deceased. Mr. Gray's assistant while recognizing that the work was done in the public interest did not feel he could certify because there was no wrtten order. From the notes of the late Mr. Gray it appears that the work was done in the public interest and while there was no written order it ought to be paid to the contractors. It is on his recommendation as appearing in his notes that this amount is asked for.
Juniper island wharf, $1,500. [DOT]
What is this for?

There is a very great deal of traffic upon these waters and Juniper island is a distributing point. A deputation waited on me urging this work and I am informed there is a very large commercial business done there.

You have as much right to put a wharf there as you have to put a wharf on any little island in a small lake.
Lakefield-reconstruction of wharf, &c., $4,050.
Was that a government wharf before ?

Yes.
Little Current-improvement of northern channel in Georgian bay, $50,000.

This is under contract, it is improving the channel.
Miagnetawan river-improvement of navigation above Kearny, $3,000.

There is quite a considerable stretch of navigation here.
Michipiooten, Lake Superior-wharf on Michipicoten river, $3,000.
On whose property will this be erected ?

On government property, we have not acquired the site yet.
Montreal river-wharf on Lake Temiska-ming, $3,000.	[DOT]

This is to pay land damages from floods which will be caused by the construction of a dam at Latchford to improve navigation.

Tiffin harbour-improvements, $50,000.
How much will be spent altogether at Tiffin ?
We think $50,000 will be all we can do this year.
There is $75,000 in the main estimates, so there will be $125,000.

Yes, this year.
Tobermory harbour-glance booms, $3,600.
This a harbour of refuge, and this is to prevent the boats running on the rocks as they come in.
Is the work at Slatcha-dash to be done out of the general vote of $300,000 for dredging in Ontario and Quebec ?
Yes.
Does the minister propose to dredge also in the Coldwater river ?
Yes.
Has there been any investigation of the Port Credit harbour in ithe last few weeks.
Yes, I gave instructions to have an investigation made.
I want to impress the necessity of having dredging done there this summer if possible.

I had that in mind about the dredging. The great trouble Is that the government of Ontario 50 years ago created a company as was apparently the practice at that time and gave over the foreshore, the harbour and everything. The company owning the wharf has allowed it to fall into decay.
Lesser Slave river

to complete urgent provisional improvements, $5,000.
What are you doing here ?

Improving the navigation ; there is a steamer running and a considerable amount of traffic.
Spiillumoheen river-repairs -to bank protection works a-t Enderby, $2,500.

This is the ordinary bank protection work, protecting the river channel. .
Dredging-Quebec and Ontario, $300,000.

How will this be divided as between Quebec and Ontario ?
Mr. PUGSLEY'. On the close of the session I intend to take the matter up with the chief engineer and the deputy, apportioning it to the different works according to our best judgment.
Thompson river improvements, $10,000.
Mr. FOWLER, What is that ?
This is on the North Thompson river.

There are no boats there except a small boat that may go up two or three times a year with supplies for the lumber company. This is simply for the benefit of an American lumber company having a mill at Kamloops.
It is to improve navigation.
It is to help them in driving logs. It is nothing but a private enterprise and has nothing to do with the public at all.
It is difficult in a new country always to draw the line.
I know all about the North Thompson river, and I know that the $10,000 is simply for the benefit of that private enterprise.
Is the minister getting new dredge plants?

We have not matured our plans yet. We are thinking that instead of buying one or more dredges, we may build two or three. We are taking the vote with the view of getting dredging plant either the one way or the other. We want additional dredges in the lower provinces and in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia.
Will tenders be called for the construction?
Yes.
There is a shipbuilding plant at Collingwood. They should be given a chance to build the dredges.
What is this item of $3,000 for clearing waterway of obstructions of Upper Lilloet river?

It is to he applied in removing from the river at its outlet the remains of an old dam, one or two piers, gravel and some boulders, with the view of facilitating the discharge from the lake, so as to mitigate the overflow of the adjoining lands and improve navigation.
Does the government intend erecting the monuments to the memory of the late D'Arcy McGee and George Brown?
Nothing has been done yet, hut we propose to place this work under the charge of the advisory art council who have to do with the erection of a monument in memory of Lafontaine and Baldwin.
Have the changes been made in the item in which my hon. friend from Brantford was interested?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is noted for .amendment on concurrence. The memorandum is in the hands of the clerk of the House, and our attention will be called to it when the item is reached.
I see an item of $4,000 additional for steam communication between Prince Edward Island, Cape Breton and Newfoundland. What ports will these boats touch ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The wording of the item would admit the service being made to any port in Prince Edward Island. I am not aware of any special arrangements.
. Mr. A. MARTIN (Queens). I would like to know whether New London and Rustico are included in this service. I wish to impress on the minister the fact that both those sections, being on the north side and without railway communication, are the mosit neglected parts of Prince Edward Island as regards communication.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
Will the Minister of Finance tell us if there are to be any further supplementary estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To the best of my knowledge and belief, no.
Not this session?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
What business will be taken up in the morning?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: After routine business a motion will be made for Supply. I understand that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) wishes to draw attention to a matter.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 1.47 a.m., Friday.
